at the slingshot stage, since the binary has shot out all the stars with small impact parameters which
might collide with it. It appeared that two SBH would never merge. This fact was called the ﬁnal parsec

plex shapes the stars with small impact parameters appear again and again. The SBH binary continues

Theory
Q3-1
English (Oﬃcial)
Space Debris
Introduction
In more than half a century of space operations quite a large number of man-made objects have been
amassed near Earth. The objects that do not serve any particular purpose are called space debris. The
most attention is usually paid to the larger debris objects, i.e. defunct satellites and spent rocket upper
stages, which stay in orbit after delivering their payload. Collisions of such objects with each other may
result in thousands of fragments endangering all current space missions.
There is a well-known hypothetical scenario, according to which certain collisions may cause a cascade
where each subsequent collision generates more space debris that increase the likelihood of new col-
lisions. Such a chain reaction, resulting in the loss of all near-Earth satellites and making impossible
further space programs, is called the Kessler syndrome.
To prevent such undesirable outcome special missions are planned to remove large debris object from
their present orbits either by tugging them to the Earth's atmosphere or to graveyard orbits. To this end
a specially designed spacecraft – a space tug – must capture a debris object. However, before capturing
an uncontrolled object it is important to understand its rotational dynamics.
We suggest you to take part in planning of such a mission and ﬁnd out how the rotational dynamics of a
debris object changes in time under the inﬂuence of different factors.
Rocket Stage Schematic
The debris object to be considered is a "Kerbodyne 42" rocket upper stage, whose schematic is shown in
Fig. 1. The circle line in Fig. 1 marks the outline of a spherical fuel tank.
Fig. 1: "Kerbodyne 42" upper stage
We introduce a body-ﬁxed reference frame 𝐶𝑥𝑦with the origin in the center of mass 𝐶, 𝑥being the
symmetry axis of the stage, and 𝑦perpendicular to 𝑥. The inertia moments with respect to 𝑥and 𝑦axes
are 𝐽𝑥and 𝐽𝑦(𝐽𝑥< 𝐽𝑦).
Part A. Rotation (3.8 points).
Consider an arbitrary initial rotation of the stage with angular momentum 𝐿(Fig. 2), where 𝜃is the angle
between the symmetry axis and the direction of angular momentum. Fuel tank at this point is assumed
to be empty. No forces or torques act upon the stage.

Space Debris
APhO 2017
Introduction
In more than half a century of space operations quite a large number of man-made objects have
been amassed near Earth. The objects that do not serve any particular purpose are called space
debris. The most attention is usually paid to the larger debris objects, i.e. defunct satellites
and spent rocket upper stages, which stay in orbit after delivering their payload. Collisions
of such objects with each other may result in thousands of fragments endangering all current
space missions.
There is a well-known hypothetical scenario, according to which certain collisions may cause a
cascade where each subsequent collision generates more space debris that increase the likelihood
of new collisions. Such a chain reaction, resulting in the loss of all near-Earth satellites and
making impossible further space programs, is called the Kessler syndrome.
To prevent such undesirable outcome special missions are planned to remove large debris ob-
ject from their present orbits either by tugging them to the Earth’s atmosphere or to graveyard
orbits. To this end a specially designed spacecraft – a space tug – must capture a debris object.
However, before capturing an uncontrolled object it is important to understand its rotational
dynamics.
We suggest you to take part in planning of such a mission and ﬁnd out how the rotational
dynamics of a debris object changes in time under the inﬂuence of diﬀerent factors.
Rocket Stage Schematic
The debris object to be considered is a “Kerbodyne 42” rocket upper stage, whose schematic
is shown in Fig. 1. The circle line in Fig. 1 marks the outline of a spherical fuel tank.

Theoretical Question – T1 
 
Mechanics of a Deformable Lattice 
(Total Marks : 20) 
 
Here we study a deformable lattice hanging in gravity which acts as a deformable physical 
pendulum. It has only one degree of freedom, i.e. only one way to deform it and the 
configuration is fully described by an angle . Such structures have been studied by famous 
physicist James Maxwell in 19th century, and some surprising behaviors have been 
discovered recently. 
As shown in the figure 1, N2 identical triangular plates (red triangle) are freely hinged by 
identical rods and form an N × N lattice (N > 1).  The joints at the vertices are denoted by 
small circles. The sides of the equilateral triangles and the rods have the same length l.  The 
dashed lines in the figure represent four tubes; each tube confines N vertices (grey circles) on 
the edge and the N vertices can slide in the tube, i.e. the tube is like a sliding rail.  
The four tubes are connected in a diamond shape with two angles fixed at 60◦ and another 
two angles at 120◦ as shown in Figure 1.  Each plate has a uniform density with mass M, and 
the other parts of the system are massless.  The configuration of the lattice is uniquely 
determined by the angle α, where 0° ≤𝛼≤60° (please see the examples of different angle 
α in Figure 1).  The system is hung vertically like a “curtain” with the top tube fixed along 
the horizontal direction.  
The coordinate system is shown in Figure 2.  The zero level of the potential energy is 
defined at y = 0.  A triangular plate is denoted by a pair of indices (m,n), where m, n = 0, 1, 2, 
· · ·, N − 1 representing the order in the x and y directions respectively.  A(m,n), B(m,n) and 
C(m,n) denote the positions of the 3 vertices of the triangle (m,n). The top-left vertex, A(0, 
0) (the big black circle), is fixed. 
The motion of the whole system is confined in the x-y plane. The moment of inertia of a 
uniform equilateral triangular plate about its center of mass is I = Ml2/12. The free fall 
acceleration is g. Please use Ek and Ep to denote kinetic energy and potential energy 
respectively.

Theoretical Question – T3 
 
 Magnetic Field Effects on Superconductors 
(Total Marks: 20) 
 
 
 
 
An electron is an elementary particle which carries electric charge and an intrinsic magnetic 
moment related to its spin angular momentum. Due to Coulomb interactions, electrons in 
vacuum are repulsive to each other. However, in some metals, the net force between electrons 
can become attractive due to the lattice vibrations. When the temperature of the metal is low 
enough, lower than some critical temperature Tc, electrons with opposite momenta and 
opposite spins can form pairs called Cooper pairs. By forming Cooper pairs, each electron 
reduces its energy by  compared to a freely propagating electron in the metal which has 
energy 
2
e
2
p
m , where p is the momentum and 
e
m  is the mass of an electron. The Cooper pairs 
can flow without resistance and the metal becomes a superconductor. 
 
However, even at temperatures lower than Tc, superconductivity can be destroyed if the 
superconductor is under the influence of an external magnetic field. In this problem, you are 
going to work out how Cooper pairs can be destroyed by external magnetic fields through two 
effects.  
 
The first is called the paramagnetic effect, in which all the electrons can lower their energy by 
aligning the electron magnetic moments parallel to the magnetic field instead of forming 
Cooper pairs with opposite spins.  
 
The second is called the diamagnetic effect, in which increasing the magnetic field will 
change the orbital motion of the Cooper pairs and increase their energy. When the applied 
magnetic field is stronger than a critical value Bc, this increase in energy becomes higher than 
2. As a result, the electrons do not prefer forming Cooper pairs. 
 
Recently, a type of superconductor called Ising superconductors was discovered. These 
superconductors can survive even when the applied magnetic field is as strong as 60 Tesla, 
comparable to the largest magnetic fields which can be created in laboratories. You will work 
out why Ising superconductors can overcome both the paramagnetic and the diamagnetic 
effects of the magnetic fields.

Question 1  
 
The fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE) was discovered by D. C. Tsui and H. 
Stormer at Bell Labs in 1981.  In the experiment electrons were confined in two 
dimensions on the GaAs side by the interface potential of a GaAs/AlGaAs 
heterojunction fabricated by A. C. Gossard (here we neglect the thickness of the 
two-dimensional electron layer).  A strong uniform magnetic field 𝐵𝐵 was applied 
perpendicular to the two-dimensional electron system. As illustrated in Figure 1, when 
a current 𝐼𝐼 was passing through the sample, the voltage 𝑉𝑉H across the current path 
exhibited an unexpected quantized plateau (corresponding to a Hall resistance 𝑅𝑅H =
3ℎ/𝑒𝑒2) at sufficiently low temperatures. The appearance of the plateau would imply 
the presence of fractionally charged quasiparticles in the system, which we analyze 
below. For simplicity, we neglect the scattering of the electrons by random potential, 
as well as the electron spin. 
 
(a) In a classical model, two-dimensional electrons behave like charged billiard balls 
on a table. In the GaAs/AlGaAs sample, however, the mass of the electrons is 
reduced to an effective mass 𝑚𝑚∗ due to their interaction with ions. 
(i) (2 point) Write down the equation of motion of an electron in perpendicular 
electric field 𝐸𝐸ሬ⃗= −𝐸𝐸𝑦𝑦𝑦𝑦ො and magnetic field 𝐵𝐵ሬ⃗= 𝐵𝐵𝑧𝑧̂. 
(ii) (1 point) Determine the velocity 𝑣𝑣s of the electrons in the stationary case. 
(iii) (1 point) Which direction is the velocity pointing at? 
 
(b) (2 points) The Hall resistance is defined as 𝑅𝑅H = 𝑉𝑉H/𝐼𝐼. In the classical model, 
find 𝑅𝑅H as a function of the number of the electrons 𝑁𝑁 and the magnetic flux 
𝜙𝜙= 𝐵𝐵𝐵𝐵= 𝐵𝐵𝐵𝐵𝐵𝐵, where 𝐴𝐴 is the area of the sample, and 𝑊𝑊 and 𝐿𝐿 the 
effective width and length of the sample, respectively. 
 
(c) (2 points) We know that electrons move in circular orbits in the magnetic field. In 
the quantum mechanical picture, the impinging magnetic field 𝐵𝐵 could be 
viewed as creating tiny whirlpools, so-called vortices, in the sea of 
electrons—one whirlpool for each flux quantum ℎ/𝑒𝑒 of the magnetic field, 
where ℎ is the Planck's constant and 𝑒𝑒 the elementary charge of an electron. 
For the case of 𝑅𝑅H = 3ℎ/𝑒𝑒2, which was discovered by Tsui and Stormer, derive 
the ratio of the number of the electrons 𝑁𝑁 to the number of the flux quanta 𝑁𝑁𝜙𝜙, 

 
 2 / 4 
 
known as the filling factor ν. 
 
 
 
Figure 1: (a) Sketch of the experimental setup for the observation of the FQHE. As indicated, a 
current 𝐼𝐼 is passing through a two-dimensional electron system in the longitudinal direction with 
an effective length 𝐿𝐿. The Hall voltage 𝑉𝑉H is measured in the transverse direction with an effective 
width 𝑊𝑊. In addition, a uniform magnetic field 𝐵𝐵 is applied perpendicular to the plane. The 
direction of the current is given for illustrative purpose only, which may not be correct. (b) Hall 
resistance 𝑅𝑅H versus 𝐵𝐵 at four different temperatures (curves shifted for clarity) in the original 
publication on the FQHE. The features at 𝑅𝑅H = 3ℎ/𝑒𝑒2 are due to the FQHE. 
 
 
(d) (2 points) It turns out that binding an integer number of vortices (𝑛𝑛> 1) with 
each electron generates a bigger surrounding whirlpool, hence pushes away all 
other electrons. Therefore, the system can considerably reduce its electrostatic 

 
 3 / 4 
 
Coulomb energy at the corresponding filling factor. Determine the scaling 
exponent 𝛼𝛼 of the amount of energy gain for each electron Δ𝑈𝑈(𝐵𝐵) ∝𝐵𝐵α. 
 
(e) (2 points) As the magnetic field deviates from the exact filling ν = 1/𝑛𝑛 to a 
higher field, more vortices (whirlpools in the electron sea) are being created. 
They are not bound to electrons and behave like particles carrying effectively 
positive charges, hence known as quasiholes, compared to the negatively charged 
electrons. The amount of charge deficit in any of these quasiholes amounts to 
exactly 1/𝑛𝑛 of an electronic charge. An analogous argument can be made for 
magnetic fields slightly below ν and the creation of quasielectrons of negative 
charge 𝑒𝑒∗= −𝑒𝑒/𝑛𝑛. At the quantized Hall plateau of 𝑅𝑅H = 3ℎ/𝑒𝑒2, calculate the 
amount of change in 𝐵𝐵 that corresponds to the introduction of exactly one 
fractionally charged quasihole. (When their density is low, the quasiparticles are 
confined by the random potential generated by impurities and imperfections, 
hence the Hall resistance remains quantized for a finite range of 𝐵𝐵.) 
 
(f) In Tsui et al. experiment, 
the magnetic field corresponding to the center of the quantized Hall plateau 
𝑅𝑅H = 3ℎ/𝑒𝑒2, 𝐵𝐵1/3 = 15 Tesla, 
the effective mass of an electron in GaAs, 𝑚𝑚∗= 0.067 𝑚𝑚𝑒𝑒, 
the electron mass, 𝑚𝑚𝑒𝑒= 9.1 × 10−31 kg, 
Coulomb's constant, 𝑘𝑘= 9.0 × 109 N ∙m2/C2, 
the vacuum permittivity, ε0 = 1/4π𝑘𝑘= 8.854 × 10−12 F/m, 
the relative permittivity (the ratio of the permittivity of a substance to the vacuum 
permittivity) of GaAs, ε𝑟𝑟= 13, 
the elementary charge, 𝑒𝑒= 1.6 × 10−19 C, 
Planck's constant, ℎ= 6.626 × 10−34 J ∙s, and 
Boltzmann's constant, 𝑘𝑘B = 1.38 × 10−23 J/K. 
In our analysis, we have neglected several factors, whose corresponding energy               
scales, compared to Δ𝑈𝑈(𝐵𝐵) discussed in (d), are either too large to excite or too 
small to be relevant. 
(i) (1 point) Calculate the thermal energy 𝐸𝐸th at temperature 𝑇𝑇= 1.0 K. 
(ii) (2 point) The electrons spatially confined in the whirlpools (or vortices) have 
a large kinetic energy. Using the uncertainty relation, estimate the order of 
magnitude of the kinetic energy. (This amount would also be the additional 
energy penalty if we put two electrons in the same whirlpool, instead of in 
two separate whirlpools, due to Pauli exclusion principle.)  
 
(g) There are also a series of plateaus at 𝑅𝑅H = ℎ/𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖2, where 𝑖𝑖= 1, 2, 3, … in Tsui et 
al. experiment, as shown in Figure 1(b). These plateaus, known as the integer 
quantum Hall effect (IQHE), were reported previously by K. von Klitzing in 1980. 
Repeating (c)-(f) for the integer plateaus, one realizes that the novelty of the 
FQHE lies critically in the existence of fractionally charged quasiparticles. R.

(ii) (2 points) Current noise is defined as the charge fluctuations per unit of time. 
One can analyze the noise by measuring the mean square deviation of the

the discreteness of the current-carrying charges in terms of λ and τ. 
(iii) (1 point) Calculate the noise-to-current ratio 𝑆𝑆𝐼𝐼/𝐼𝐼B, which was verified by R.

Question 1
The fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE) was discovered by D. C. Tsui and
H. Stormer at Bell Labs in 1981. In the experiment electrons were conﬁned in
two dimensions on the GaAs side by the interface potential of a GaAs/AlGaAs
heterojunction fabricated by A. C. Gossard (here we neglect the thickness of the
two-dimensional electron layer). A strong uniform magnetic ﬁeld B was applied
perpendicular to the two-dimensional electron system. As illustrated in Figure
1, when a current I was passing through the sample, the voltage VH across the
current path exhibited an unexpected quantized plateau (corresponding to a Hall
resistance RH = 3h/e2) at sufﬁciently low temperatures. The appearance of the
plateau would imply the presence of fractionally charged quasiparticles in the
system, which we analyze below. For simplicity, we neglect the scattering of the

Question 2 
 
How are aurora ignited by the solar wind? 
 
Figure 1 
The following questions are designed to guide you to find the answer one step by one step. 
Background information of the interaction between the solar wind and the Earth's magnetic 
field 
It is well known that the Earth has a substantial magnetic field. The field lines defining the 
structure of the Earth's magnetic field is similar to that of a simple bar magnet, as shown in Figure 
2. The Earth's magnetic field is disturbed by the solar wind, whichis a high-speed stream of hot 
plasma. (The plasma is the quasi-neutralionized gas.)The plasma blows outward from the Sun and 
varies in intensity with the amount of surface activity on the Sun. The solar wind compresses the 
Earth's magnetic field. On the other hand, the Earth's magnetic field shields the Earth from much 
of the solar wind. When the solar wind encounters the Earth's magnetic field, it is deflected like 
water around the bow of a ship, as illustrated in Figure 3. 
 
Figure 2 

 
Question 2 
 
 
Figure 3 
The curved surface at which the solar wind is first deflected is called the bow shock. The 
corresponding region behind the bow shock andfront of the Earth's magnetic field is called 
themagnetosheath. The region surroundedby the solar wind is called the magnetosphere.The 
Earth's magnetic field largely prevents the solar wind from enteringthe magnetosphere. The 
contact region between the solar wind and the Earth's magnetic field is named the magnetopause. 
The location of the magnetopause is mainly determined by the intensity and the magnetic field 
direction of the solar wind. When the magnetic field in the solar wind is antiparallel to the Earth's 
magnetic field, magnetic reconnection as shown in Figure 4 takes place at the dayside 
magnetopause, which allows some charged particles ofthe solar wind in the region "A" to move 
into the magnetotail "P" on the night side as illustrated in Figure 5. A powerful solar wind can 
push the dayside magnetopause tovery close to the Earth, which could cause a high-orbit satellite 
(such as a geosynchronous satellite) to be fully exposed to the solar wind. The energetic particles 
in the solar wind could damage high-tech electronic components in a satellite.Therefore, it 
isimportant to study the motion of charged particles in magnetic fields, which will give an answer 
of the aurora generation and could help us to understand the mechanism of the interaction between 
the solar wind and the Earth's magnetic field.

children.text: A phase point specifies the coordinate and momentum of a system, and its trajectory has arrows in the direction of time. For a one-coordinate system the phase portrait is a collection of curves in a two-dimensional plane. Unless specified otherwise use axes \((x,p)\), with \(p=m\dot x\), and neglect air resistance. For a pendulum use \((\alpha,\dot\alpha)\), where \(\alpha\) is measured from the downward vertical.
Draw the phase trajectory of a free particle reflecting elastically from walls at \(x=\pm L/2\).

Draw a harmonic-oscillator phase trajectory and indicate its time direction.

A mass \(m\) at the end of a massless rigid rod of length \(L\) swings in gravity \(g\). Draw its phase portrait at arbitrary angle. How many qualitatively different non-equilibrium trajectory types occur, and what conditions distinguish them?

A block of mass \(m\) on a horizontal surface is attached to a spring of constant \(k\). Static and kinetic friction coefficients both equal \(\mu\). Initially \(x=A_0>0\), velocity zero. Write its equation of motion.

children.text: The speed is constant between impacts, giving horizontal segments \(p=\pm p_0\), \(-L/2<x<L/2\). At each wall momentum reverses instantaneously. The top segment runs right and the bottom segment left, with the wall jumps closing a clockwise rectangle.
Energy conservation gives \(p^2/(2m)+kx^2/2=E\), or \[\frac{x^2}{2E/k}+\frac{p^2}{2mE}=1.\] The semiaxes are \(\sqrt{2E/k}\) in x and \(\sqrt{2mE}\) in p.
Draw the ellipse centred on the origin. At positive p the coordinate increases, so the trajectory is clockwise. The origin itself is the equilibrium point.

Energy is \(E=mL^2\dot\alpha^2/2+mgL(1-\cos\alpha)\). There are three types: closed librations for \(0<E<2mgL\), separatrices for \(E=2mgL\), and continuous rotations for \(E>2mgL\). Plot both rotational directions and both branches of each separatrix. Centres are at \(\alpha=2n\pi\), saddles at \((2n+1)\pi\). The separatrix approaches a top equilibrium only asymptotically. Equilibrium points are excluded from the count.

nodes.alt: Original pendulum energy and phase portrait showing oscillations, separatrices and rotations.

children.text: While moving, \[m\ddot x=-kx-\mu mg\,\operatorname{sgn}(\dot x).\] At rest it remains stuck if \(|kx|\le\mu mg\). The moving equation alone must not be used to force motion through the sticking region.
B2. Damped phase portrait and equilibria

Define \(c=\mu mg/k\), \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\). For positive velocity, \((x+c)^2+(p/(m\omega_0))^2\) is constant. For negative velocity replace \(x+c\) by \(x-c\). Join alternating half-ellipses at turning points with clockwise arrows. Their centres are \((-c,0)\) and \((c,0)\), but the actual static equilibria comprise the entire segment \(p=0,|x|\le c\).

nodes.alt: Original clockwise sliding-friction phase trajectory with alternating shifted half-ellipses.

children.text: It need not stop at zero. Static friction permits any \(-c\le x_f\le c\), whose width is \(2c=2\mu mg/k\).
Each half-cycle reduces turning-distance magnitude by \(2c\). A full cycle therefore gives \(\Delta A=4c=4\mu mg/k\).

Each moving half-cycle lasts \(\pi/\omega_0\). Thus \(t_n=nT\), \(T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}\), and \(A(t_n)=A_0-4n\mu mg/k\), until sticking interrupts the next half-cycle. The envelope is linear rather than exponential.
B5. Motion graph and cycle count

Draw sinusoidal arcs around alternating shifted centres, under a linearly decreasing envelope, then a horizontal line at the final position in \([-c,c]\). The rough full-cycle estimate is \(N\simeq A_0/(4c)=kA_0/(4\mu mg)\), which is not an exact integer count near the last partial cycle. More precisely, if \(A_0>c\), the number of moving half-cycles is \(\lceil(A_0-c)/(2c)\rceil\). If \(A_0\le c\), the block never starts.

The biprism consists of a grounded cylindrical wire mesh with a thin central filament \(F\), directed into the figure. \(S_1,S_2\) are virtual sources separated by \(d\). The source-to-biprism distance is \(\ell\), and the biprism-to-screen distance is \(L\). The diagram is not to scale. Experiments were performed by Mollenstedt and colleagues, Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi, and Tonomura and colleagues.

solution.text:
Question 2: Electron biprism
a. Cylindrical potential
For line charge density \(\lambda_q\), Gauss's law gives \(E_r=\lambda_q/(2\pi\epsilon_0r)\). Integrate with \(V(b)=0\) and eliminate \(\lambda_q\) using \(V(a)=V_a\):
\[V(r)=\frac{\lambda_q}{2\pi\epsilon_0}\ln\frac br=V_a\frac{\ln(b/r)}{\ln(b/a)},\qquad r=\sqrt{x^2+z^2}.\]
b. Transverse impulse
With electron charge \(-e\), the force is \(F_x=e\,\partial V/\partial x=-eV_ax/[(x^2+z^2)\ln(b/a)]\). To leading small-deflection order, treat \(x\) and \(v_z\) as constant during transit. The near-filament straight-line approximation extends the impulse integral to infinite limits:
\[\Delta p_x=\frac1{v_z}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F_x\,dz=-\operatorname{sgn}(x)\frac{\pi eV_a}{v_z\ln(b/a)}.\]
\[|k_x|=\frac{2\pi}{h}|\Delta p_x|=\frac{2\pi^2 eV_a}{hv_z\ln(b/a)}.\]
Equivalently, solve the transverse equation of motion for the small slope \(|dx/dz|=\pi eV_a/[mv_z^2\ln(b/a)]\) in a nonrelativistic trajectory treatment, then use \(k_x/k_z\simeq dx/dz\). In the relativistic form use \(p_z=\gamma mv_z\), so the same impulse-to-wave-vector result follows. The positive source result is the magnitude, although an intermediate impulse is evaluated at positive \(x\) with an inconsistent sign.
c. de Broglie wavelengths
Nonrelativistically, \(p^2/(2m)=eV_0\). Relativistically, total energy is \(mc^2+eV_0\), so \(p^2c^2=(mc^2+eV_0)^2-m^2c^4\). Hence
\[\lambda_\mathrm{nr}=\frac h{\sqrt{2meV_0}},\qquad \lambda_\mathrm{rel}=\frac h{\sqrt{2meV_0\left(1+\dfrac{eV_0}{2mc^2}\right)}}.\]
d. Numerical results and geometry
\[|k_x|\simeq3.46\times10^7\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}.\]
The two symmetric plane-wave components have transverse wave vectors \(+k_x\) and \(-k_x\), so their interference phase difference is \(2k_xx\). The fringe spacing is
\[s=\frac\pi{|k_x|}\simeq9.07\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm m=90.7\,\mathrm{nm}.\]
With a spherical incident wave, geometric divergence makes the fringe spacing larger than the plane-wave result. This qualitative comparison remains self-review.
\[\lambda_\mathrm{nr}\simeq5.47\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm m,\qquad\lambda_\mathrm{rel}\simeq5.34\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm m,\]
\[100\frac{\lambda_\mathrm{nr}-\lambda_\mathrm{rel}}{\lambda_\mathrm{rel}}\simeq2.4\%.\]
The official apparent-double-slit estimate inserts its d.ii fringe spacing and relativistic wavelength into \(s=\lambda_\mathrm{rel}(\ell+L)/d\), giving \(d\simeq1.03\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm m\). The numerical field explicitly follows that substitution.
Source-model caveat: the source mixes the plane-wave fringe spacing with the virtual-point-source formula in the last estimate. A self-consistent spherical-source geometry instead gives \(d=2\ell|k_x|/k_z\) and a larger spacing \(s=\pi(\ell+L)/(\ell|k_x|)\). Using the supplied relativistic wavelength gives \(d\simeq1.47\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm m\). Thus the last source value is an official estimate under its stated substitution, not a claim that both wavefront models have the same spacing. Let observer-lens distance be \(D_L\), observer-source distance \(D_S>D_L\), and apparent angular Einstein radius be \(\theta_E\). Use \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{SI}\) and \(c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\).
a. Aligned lens geometry
Draw the ideal observer-lens-point-source layout. Show a deflected ray, its deflection angle, Einstein radius, apparent angular radius and measurable distances.
b. Perfect alignment image
Sketch the observed image for exact alignment.
c. Misalignment image
Sketch the image and source-lens geometry when the three bodies are not aligned.
d.escape. Newtonian escape speed
Derive escape speed from distance \(r\) from point mass \(M\).
d.radius. Schwarzschild radius
Set that escape speed equal to c to derive the Schwarzschild-radius expression. Explain the scope of this argument.
e. Radius from deflection
In the aligned case, find \(r_S\) from measured \(\alpha,r_E\).
f. Angular approximation choice
For a lens of a few solar masses at a distance of a few \(10^{18}\,\mathrm m\), and a source a few times farther away, choose independently for \(\alpha\) and \(\theta_E\): large and requiring exact trigonometry, small and permitting small-angle approximations, or irrelevant.
g. Radius from measurable distances
Use the preceding approximation to express \(r_S\) in terms of \(\theta_E,D_S,D_L\).
h. Einstein angular radius
A lens of \(6.0\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\), at \(2.6\times10^{18}\,\mathrm m\), passes in front of a star at \(9.2\times10^{18}\,\mathrm m\). Find the Einstein angular radius at exact alignment.

solution.text:
Gravitational lensing
a. Aligned lens geometry
Place observer, lens and source on an axis, with the lens between the others. Draw a ray reaching transverse radius \(r_E\) at the lens plane, then bending towards the observer. Label \(\theta_E\) at the observer, total bend \(\alpha\) at the lens, distances \(D_L,D_S,D_S-D_L\). The source-side angle is \(\alpha-\theta_E\). Rotational symmetry creates equivalent rays at all azimuths.

b. Perfect alignment image
Rotational symmetry turns a point image into a circular Einstein ring, centred on the projected lens position, with angular radius \(\theta_E\). A finite-size source broadens the ring.
c. Misalignment image
For an ideal point source and point lens there are two images, on opposite sides of the lens along the line to the unlensed source. For a small-angle source offset \(\beta\), the lens equation is \(\beta=\theta-\theta_E^2/\theta\), with roots \(\theta_\pm=[\beta\pm\sqrt{\beta^2+4\theta_E^2}]/2\). A resolved extended source produces distorted arcs, rather than a complete ring. Show the two rays in the plane containing observer, lens and source. The official marking notes favour arcs and discuss incomplete rings. Those describe an extended or resolved source. For the ideal point-source, point-lens model, the two-image lens-equation result above is the consistent limit. Compare the geometry as well as the sketch.
d.escape. Newtonian escape speed
Zero asymptotic kinetic energy requires \(mv_{esc}^2/2-GMm/r=0\), so \(v_{esc}=\sqrt{2GM/r}\).
d.radius. Schwarzschild radius
The substitution gives \(r_S=2GM/c^2\), the same radius as in general relativity. The Newtonian argument reproduces the expression but does not derive an event horizon or the behaviour of light inside it.
e. Radius from deflection
Because \(\alpha=2r_S/r_E\), \(r_S=\alpha r_E/2\).
f. Angular approximation choice
Both angles are very small. Small-angle approximations for sine and tangent are valid for both. Neither angle is irrelevant to the geometry.
g. Radius from measurable distances
\(r_E\simeq D_L\theta_E\), and \(\alpha\simeq\theta_E+r_E/(D_S-D_L)=\theta_ED_S/(D_S-D_L)\). Therefore \[r_S=\frac{\theta_E^2D_LD_S}{2(D_S-D_L)}.\]
h. Einstein angular radius
\[\theta_E=\sqrt{\frac{4GM}{c^2}\frac{D_S-D_L}{D_LD_S}}=7.0\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad},\] about 0.014 arcseconds.

statement.text:
Conductors in Conducting Liquid
Two conducting bodies are immersed in a uniform dielectric, weakly conducting liquid and held at constant voltage difference. Use vacuum permittivity \(\epsilon_0\) and permeability \(\mu_0\) unless stated otherwise. Ignore edge effects for the long cylinders introduced in part 4.
1. Line-charge field
Find the electric field at radial distance \(r\) from an infinite line charge \(\lambda\) in vacuum.
2. Line-charge potential
Write \(V(r)=f(r)+K\). Find \(f(r)\).
3. Two-line potential and surfaces
An infinite line at \((x,y)=(-b,0)\) has charge \(+\lambda\), and one at \((b,0)\) has \(-\lambda\). Both are parallel to z. Find potential, setting it to zero at the origin, and sketch equipotential surfaces.
4. Conducting-cylinder potential
Two identical cylinders have radius \(3a\), length \(l\gg3a\), and axes at \(x=\pm5a,y=0\), parallel to z. A battery holds the left cylinder at higher potential by \(V_0\). Find potential in all regions, zero at the origin.
5. Cylinder capacitance
Find the capacitance of the pair.
6. Leakage current
Fully immerse both cylinders in liquid of conductivity \(\sigma\) and permittivity \(\epsilon_0\). Find total current between them.
7.R. Pair resistance
Find resistance of the liquid path.
7.RC. Resistance-capacitance product
Find the product RC.
8. Magnetic field
Find the magnetic field due to the liquid current in part 6, with permeability \(\mu_0\). Use the ideal infinite-length, symmetric current-return model of the source, and explain any angular branch convention.

children.text: Gauss's law on a coaxial cylinder gives \(\mathbf E=\lambda\hat{\mathbf r}/(2\pi\epsilon_0r)\).
Integrating \(-E_r\) gives \(f(r)=-\lambda\ln(r/r_*)/(2\pi\epsilon_0)\), where any reference length \(r_*\) is absorbed in K. There is no finite choice \(V(\infty)=0\) for an isolated infinite line.

Superposition gives \[V=\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\ln\frac{(x-b)^2+y^2}{(x+b)^2+y^2}.\] Fixed nonzero potential means a fixed ratio of distances, hence coaxial families of circular cylinders parallel to z. The zero-potential surface is the plane \(x=0\).

The appropriate equivalent line charges lie at \(x=\pm4a\). Their distance ratio on each surface is 3 or 1/3, and \(\lambda=\pi\epsilon_0V_0/\ln3\). In the exterior, \[V=\frac{V_0}{4\ln3}\ln\frac{(x-4a)^2+y^2}{(x+4a)^2+y^2}.\] Inside the left cylinder \(V=+V_0/2\), inside the right \(V=-V_0/2\). The line-charge expression must not be continued into the metal.

nodes.alt: Original two-line-charge construction of a cylindrical equipotential surface with distances l1 and l2.

children.text: The charge on the positive cylinder is \(\lambda l\), so \[C=\pi\epsilon_0l/\ln3.\]
The stationary potential obeys the same Laplace problem. Since \(\mathbf j=\sigma\mathbf E\), its flux is \(\sigma/\epsilon_0\) times electric displacement flux. Thus \[I=\pi\sigma lV_0/\ln3.\]
Geometry cancels: \(RC=\epsilon_0/\sigma\), the dielectric relaxation time.

Translational symmetry gives an axial field \(\mathbf B=B_z\hat{\mathbf z}\). Ampere's law yields \(\partial_yB_z=\mu_0j_x\) and \(\partial_xB_z=-\mu_0j_y\). In the central strip \(|x|<a\), with the source's symmetry \(B_z(x,0)=0\), \[B_z=\frac{\mu_0\sigma V_0}{2\ln3}\left[\arctan\frac y{4a+x}+\arctan\frac y{4a-x}\right].\] A rectangular Ampere loop symmetric about \(y=0\) gives the same result by integrating \(j_x\) across it. Away from this strip, continue the angular functions on the appropriate exterior branches rather than blindly using principal arctangents. A physical finite cylinder and its battery leads require the return-current geometry, omitted by the ideal edge-free model. The source's unqualified principal-arctangent formula is therefore used only in its valid central region here.

solution.text:
Conductors in Conducting Liquid
1. Line-charge field
Gauss's law on a coaxial cylinder gives \(\mathbf E=\lambda\hat{\mathbf r}/(2\pi\epsilon_0r)\).
2. Line-charge potential
Integrating \(-E_r\) gives \(f(r)=-\lambda\ln(r/r_*)/(2\pi\epsilon_0)\), where any reference length \(r_*\) is absorbed in K. There is no finite choice \(V(\infty)=0\) for an isolated infinite line.
3. Two-line potential and surfaces
Superposition gives \[V=\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\ln\frac{(x-b)^2+y^2}{(x+b)^2+y^2}.\] Fixed nonzero potential means a fixed ratio of distances, hence coaxial families of circular cylinders parallel to z. The zero-potential surface is the plane \(x=0\).
4. Conducting-cylinder potential
The appropriate equivalent line charges lie at \(x=\pm4a\). Their distance ratio on each surface is 3 or 1/3, and \(\lambda=\pi\epsilon_0V_0/\ln3\). In the exterior, \[V=\frac{V_0}{4\ln3}\ln\frac{(x-4a)^2+y^2}{(x+4a)^2+y^2}.\] Inside the left cylinder \(V=+V_0/2\), inside the right \(V=-V_0/2\). The line-charge expression must not be continued into the metal.

5. Cylinder capacitance
The charge on the positive cylinder is \(\lambda l\), so \[C=\pi\epsilon_0l/\ln3.\]
6. Leakage current
The stationary potential obeys the same Laplace problem. Since \(\mathbf j=\sigma\mathbf E\), its flux is \(\sigma/\epsilon_0\) times electric displacement flux. Thus \[I=\pi\sigma lV_0/\ln3.\]
7.R. Pair resistance
\(R=V_0/I=\ln3/(\pi\sigma l)\).
7.RC. Resistance-capacitance product
Geometry cancels: \(RC=\epsilon_0/\sigma\), the dielectric relaxation time.
8. Magnetic field
Translational symmetry gives an axial field \(\mathbf B=B_z\hat{\mathbf z}\). Ampere's law yields \(\partial_yB_z=\mu_0j_x\) and \(\partial_xB_z=-\mu_0j_y\). In the central strip \(|x|<a\), with the source's symmetry \(B_z(x,0)=0\), \[B_z=\frac{\mu_0\sigma V_0}{2\ln3}\left[\arctan\frac y{4a+x}+\arctan\frac y{4a-x}\right].\] A rectangular Ampere loop symmetric about \(y=0\) gives the same result by integrating \(j_x\) across it. Away from this strip, continue the angular functions on the appropriate exterior branches rather than blindly using principal arctangents. A physical finite cylinder and its battery leads require the return-current geometry, omitted by the ideal edge-free model. The source's unqualified principal-arctangent formula is therefore used only in its valid central region here.

statement.text:
The Drag on a Falling Magnet
A clear and detailed discussion of eddy currents was first provided by the British physicist Sir James H. Jeans (1877–1946) in The mathematical theory of electricity and magnetism (1925). The present problem is based on electricity and magnetism.


A small magnet with dipole moment of magnitude \(p\) and mass \(m\) is dropped through a very long vertically held non-magnetic metallic tube as shown in Figure 1, which is not to scale. In general the fall is governed by
\[m\ddot z=mg-k\dot z.\tag{1}\]
Here \(g\) is gravitational acceleration. The damping parameter \(k\) is due to the generation of eddy currents in the tube.
I.1 (0.5 point)
Obtain the terminal velocity \(v_T\) of the magnet.
I.2 (1.0 point)
Obtain the position \(z(t)\) of the magnet at time \(t\). Take \(v(0)=0\) and \(z(0)=0\).
To understand the fall, consider in I.3 to I.8 a simplified problem: the magnet falls axially towards a fixed non-magnetic metallic ring of radius \(a\), resistance \(R\), and inductance \(L\), as shown in Figure 2. Ignore radiation effects.

Use cylindrical coordinates \((\rho,\varphi,z)\). The \(z\)-axis is the ring axis, the magnet is initially at rest at the origin, and the ring centre is at distance \(z_0\) from the origin. Cartesian axes \((x,y,z)\) are also shown. The dipole moment is \(\mathbf p=p\hat{\mathbf k}\), where \(\hat{\mathbf k}\) is the unit vector in the positive \(z\) direction. Assume the magnetic moment remains in that direction. When the magnet is at the origin, the axial and radial field components at \((\rho,\varphi,z)\) are
\[B_z=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{p}{(\rho^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\left(\frac{3z^2}{\rho^2+z^2}-1\right),\qquad B_\rho=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3pz\rho}{(\rho^2+z^2)^{5/2}},\]
where \(\mu_0\) is the permeability of free space.
I.3 (1.5 points)
Let the instantaneous speed of the magnet be \(v\). Obtain the magnitude of the induced emf \(e_i\) in the ring.
I.4 (1.0 point)
This emf gives rise to an induced current \(i\) in the ring. Obtain the magnitude of the instantaneous electromagnetic force \(f_{\mathrm{em}}\) on the ring in terms of \(i\).
I.5 (0.5 point)
What is the magnitude of the force on the magnet due to this ring?
I.6 (0.5 point)
Express the emf in terms of \(L\), \(R\), and \(i\). Do not solve for \(i\).
I.7 (1.0 point)
As the magnet falls it loses gravitational potential energy. Identify the three main forms of energy into which it is converted, and write down the expressions used to calculate each contribution.
I.8 (0.5 point)
Does the magnet's magnetic field do any work in this process? Answer yes or no.
Next estimate the damping parameter \(k\) due to the pipe in Eq. (1). solution.text:
Detailed answer and grading scheme
I.1
The equation of motion is \(m\ddot z=mg-k\dot z\). At terminal velocity \(\ddot z=0\) (0.2 mark), giving
\[v_T=\dot z=\frac{mg}{k}.\]
Terminal velocity: 0.3 mark.
I.2
\[\frac{dv}{dt}=g-\frac{k}{m}v(t),\qquad v(0)=z(0)=0,\]
\[v(t)=\frac{mg}{k}(1-e^{-kt/m})=\frac{dz}{dt}.\]
Velocity: 0.5 mark. Integrating
\[\int_0^z dz=\int_0^t\frac{mg}{k}(1-e^{-kt/m})\,dt,\qquad z(t)=\frac{mg}{k}\left[t+\frac{m}{k}(e^{-kt/m}-1)\right].\]
Position: 0.5 mark.
I.3. Method I
Because of the relative speed \(v\) between the magnet and ring in the magnet's field \(\mathbf B=B_z\hat{\mathbf k}+B_\rho\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}\), the induced emf is
\[e_i=\int(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l=vB_a\,2\pi a,\]
The integral and substitution receive 0.8 and 0.4 mark, respectively, where
\[B_a=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3pa(z_0-z)}{[a^2+(z_0-z)^2]^{5/2}}.\tag{2}\]
Field expression: 0.3 mark.
I.3. Method II
The magnetic flux through the ring is
\[\phi=\int_0^a B_z\,2\pi\rho\,d\rho=2\pi\int_0^a\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{\rho p}{[\rho^2+(z_0-z)^2]^{3/2}}\left[\frac{3(z_0-z)^2}{\rho^2+(z_0-z)^2}-1\right]d\rho,\]
\[\phi=\frac{\mu_0pa^2}{2[a^2+(z_0-z)^2]^{3/2}},\qquad e_i=-\frac{d\phi}{dt}=-v\frac{d\phi}{dz},\]
\[e_i=\frac{3\mu_0pa^2v(z_0-z)}{2[a^2+(z_0-z)^2]^{5/2}}.\]
The flux integral, its substitution, integrated flux, Faraday-law step, and final emf receive 0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.4 mark. The source prints a signed expression while the question requests a magnitude. Magnitudes use absolute values when the magnet has passed the ring.
I.4
The \(B_z\) component causes radially outward forces on the ring, with zero net force by symmetry (0.4 mark). Only \(B_\rho\) contributes
\[d\mathbf f_{\mathrm{em}}=i(d\mathbf l\times\mathbf B),\qquad |\mathbf f_{\mathrm{em}}|=i\,2\pi aB_a,\]
where \(B_a\) is given by Eq. (2). Force: 0.6 mark.
I.5
By Newton's third law, the ring exerts an equal and opposite force on the magnet. Its magnitude is \(f_{\mathrm{em}}\) (0.5 mark).
I.6
\[e_i=L\frac{di}{dt}+iR.\]
Circuit equation: 0.5 mark.
I.7
Potential energy is converted into kinetic energy \(mv^2/2\) (0.3 mark), magnetic energy \(Li^2/2\) (0.3 mark), and Joule loss \(i^2R\Delta t\) in time \(\Delta t\) (0.4 mark).
I.8
The magnetic field does no work in the process. The source ticks No (0.5 mark).
I.9
\[\Delta R=\frac{2\pi a}{\sigma w\Delta z'}.\]
Ring resistance: 0.5 mark.
I.10
For one ring at \(z'\), the force is \(f_{\mathrm{em}}=(2\pi a)iB'_a\), where
\[B'_a=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3pa(z'-z)}{[a^2+(z'-z)^2]^{5/2}}.\]
Field: 0.3 mark. The induced current is
\[i=\frac{e_i}{\Delta R}=\frac{\sigma we_i}{2\pi a}\Delta z'.\]
Current: 0.5 mark. Therefore the force from the entire pipe is
\[F=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{\mathrm{em}}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(B'_a)^2(2\pi a)w\sigma\,dz'\,\dot z.\]
Force integral: 0.2 mark. For the very long pipe the limits can be taken as infinite. Substitution gives
\[F=\left(\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\right)^2 18p^2a^3\pi w\sigma\dot z\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{(z'-z)^2}{[(z'-z)^2+a^2]^5}\,dz'.\]
Substitution: 0.5 mark. Let \(u=(z'-z)/a\). This is the opposite sign to the variable defined in the question, which leaves this even integral unchanged.
\[F=\left(\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\right)^2\frac{18p^2\pi\sigma w\dot z}{a^4}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{u^2}{(1+u^2)^5}\,du,\]
\[k=\left(\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\right)^2\frac{18p^2\pi\sigma w}{a^4}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{u^2}{(1+u^2)^5}\,du.\]
Damping parameter: 0.5 mark.
I.11
Given \(k=f(\mu_0,p,R_0,a)\), the dimensions are
\[[\mu_0]=I^{-2}MLT^{-2},\quad[p]=IL^2,\quad[R_0]=I^{-2}ML^2T^{-3},\quad[a]=L,\quad[k]=MT^{-1}.\]
The first three dimension statements receive 0.2, 0.1, and 0.2 mark. They give
\[k=\frac{p^2\mu_0^2}{a^4R_0}.\]
Final expression: 0.5 mark.

children.text: This problem deals with the two beam phenomena associated with light, its interference, polarization and superposition. The particular context of the problem was studied by the Indian physicist S. Pancharatnam (1934-1969).

nodes.alt: Original portrait and caption of the Indian physicist S. Pancharatnam, 1934-1969.

children.text: Consider the experimental set up as shown in Fig. (1). Two coherent monochromatic light beams (marked as beam 1 and 2), travelling in the \(z\) direction, are incident on two narrow slits and separated by a distance \(d\) (\(S_1S_2=d\)). After passing through the slits the two beams interfere and the pattern is observed on the screen \(S\). The distance between the slits and the screen is \(D\) and \(D\gg d\). Assume that the width of each slit \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) is much smaller than the wavelength of light.

nodes.alt: Figure 1. Two coherent beams travel along z through slits S1 and S2 separated by d. Screen S is a distance D away. Theta is measured from the z direction for the outgoing rays.

children.text: III.1. Two linearly polarized beams (1.0 point)
Let the beams 1 and 2 be linearly polarized at \(z=0\). The corresponding electric field vectors are given by

where \(\hat i\) is the unit vector along the x-axis, \(\omega\) is angular frequency of light and \(E_0\) is the amplitude. Find the expression for the intensity of the light \(I(\theta)\) that will be observed on the screen where \(\theta\) is the angle shown in Fig. (1). Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c\) and \(\omega\), where \(c\) is the speed of light. Also, note that the intensity is proportional to the time average of the square of the electric field. Here you may take the proportionality constant to be \(\beta\). You may ignore the attenuation in the magnitude of the electric fields with distance from the slits to any point on the screen.

A perfectly transparent glass slab of thickness \(w\) and refractive index \(\mu\) is introduced in the path of beam 1 before the slits. Find the expression for the intensity of the light \(I(\theta)\) that will be observed on the screen. Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c,\omega,\mu\) and \(w\).

An optical device (known as quarter wave plate (QWP)) is introduced in the path of beam 1, before the slits, replacing the glass slab. This device changes the polarization of the beam from the linear polarization state \(\vec E_1=\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t)\) to a circular polarization state which is given by
\[\vec E_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}[\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t)+\hat j E_0\sin(\omega t)].\tag{2}\]

Here \(\hat j\) is the unit vector along the y-axis. Assume that the device does not introduce any additional path difference and that it is perfectly transparent. Note that the tip of the electric field vector traces a circle as time elapses and hence, the beam is said to be circularly polarized. We assume that the angle \(\theta\) is small enough so that intensity from slit one does not depend on the angle \(\theta\) even for \(\hat j\) polarization.
III.3.a. Find the expression for the intensity \(I(\theta)\) of the light that will be observed on the screen. Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c\) and \(\omega\).
III.3.b. What is the maximum intensity \(I_{\max}\)?
III.3.c. What is the minimum intensity \(I_{\min}\)?

nodes.alt: Figure 2. Beam 1 passes a quarter wave plate at z=a, polarizer I between a and b, and polarizer II between b and c before slit S1. Beam 2 travels directly to slit S2.

children.text: Now consider the experimental setup (see Fig. (2)) in which beam 1 is subjected to the device (QWP) described in part 3 and a linear polarizer (marked as I), between \(z=a\) and \(z=b\), which allows only the component of the electric field parallel to an axis \(\hat i'\) to pass through. The unit vector \(\hat i'\) is defined as

Another linear polarizer (marked as II) between \(z=b\) and \(z=c\) polarizes the beam back to \(\hat i\) direction. Thus beam 1 is back to its original state of polarization. Assume that the polarizers do not introduce any path difference and are perfectly transparent.
III.4.a. Write down the expression for the electric field of beam 1 after the first polarizer at \(z=b\), \(\vec E_1(z=b)\).
III.4.b. Write down the expression for the electric field of beam 1 after the second polarizer at \(z=c\), \(\vec E_1(z=c)\).
III.4.c. What is the phase difference \(\alpha\) between the two beams at the slits?

The most general type of polarization is elliptical polarization. A convenient way of expressing elliptical polarization is to consider it as a superposition of two orthogonal linearly polarized components, i.e.
\[\vec E=\hat i'E_0\cos e\cos(\omega t)+\hat j'E_0\sin e\sin(\omega t),\tag{3}\]
where \(\hat i'\) and \(\hat j'\) and this state of polarization are depicted in Fig. 3.

nodes.alt: Figure 3. The electric-field tip traces an ellipse with principal axes i-prime and j-prime. The semiaxes are E0 cos e and E0 sin e, and the principal frame is rotated relative to i and j.

children.text: The tip of the electric field vector traces an ellipse as time elapses. Here \(e\) represents the ellipticity and is given by \(\tan e=\text{Semi-minor axis of the ellipse}/\text{Semi-major axis of the ellipse}\).

Linear polarization (Eqs. (1)) and circular polarization (Eq. (2)) are special cases of elliptical polarization (Eq. (3)). The two parameters \(\gamma\in[0,\pi]\) and \(e\in[-\pi/4,\pi/4]\) completely describe the state of polarization.

The polarization state can also be represented by a point on a sphere of unit radius called the Poincare sphere. The polarization of the beam described in Eq. (3) is represented by a point \(P\) on the Poincare sphere (see Fig. 4), then latitude \(\angle PCD=2e\) and longitude \(\angle ACD=2\gamma\). Here \(C\) is the center.

nodes.alt: Figure 4. Unit Poincare sphere centered at C. ACD is the longitude 2 gamma and DCP is the latitude 2 e of polarization point P. D lies on the equator beneath P.

children.text: Consider a point on the equator of the Poincare sphere. III.5.a. Write down the electric field \(\vec E_{\rm Eq}\) corresponding to this point. III.5.b. What is its state of polarization?
Consider a point at the north pole of the Poincare sphere. III.6.a. Write down the electric field \(\vec E_{\rm NP}\) corresponding to this point. III.6.b. What is its state of polarization?

Now consider the three polarization states of beam 1 as given in part 4. Let the initial polarization (at \(z=0\)) be represented by a point \(A_1\) on the Poincare sphere, after the optical device let the state (at \(z=a\)) be represented by point \(A_2\), and after the first polarizer (say, at \(z=b\)) let the state be represented by point \(A_3\). At \(z=c\), the polarization returns to its original state which is represented by \(A_1\). Locate these points (\(A_1,A_2,A_3\)) on the Poincare sphere.

If these three points (\(A_1,A_2,A_3\) from part (III.7)) are joined by great circles on the sphere, a triangle on the surface of the sphere is obtained. A great circle is a circle on the sphere whose center coincides with the center of the sphere. The phase difference \(\alpha\) obtained in part 4 and the area \(S\) of the curved surface enclosed by the triangle are related to each other. Relate \(S\) to \(\alpha\).
This relationship is general and was obtained by Pancharatnam and the phase difference is called the Pancharatnam phase.

statement.text:
Pancharatnam Phase
This problem deals with the two beam phenomena associated with light, its interference, polarization and superposition. The particular context of the problem was studied by the Indian physicist S. Pancharatnam (1934-1969).

Consider the experimental set up as shown in Fig. (1). Two coherent monochromatic light beams (marked as beam 1 and 2), travelling in the \(z\) direction, are incident on two narrow slits and separated by a distance \(d\) (\(S_1S_2=d\)). After passing through the slits the two beams interfere and the pattern is observed on the screen \(S\). The distance between the slits and the screen is \(D\) and \(D\gg d\). Assume that the width of each slit \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) is much smaller than the wavelength of light.

III.1. Two linearly polarized beams (1.0 point)
Let the beams 1 and 2 be linearly polarized at \(z=0\). The corresponding electric field vectors are given by
\[\vec E_1=\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t),\tag{1a}\]
\[\vec E_2=\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t),\tag{1b}\]
where \(\hat i\) is the unit vector along the x-axis, \(\omega\) is angular frequency of light and \(E_0\) is the amplitude. Find the expression for the intensity of the light \(I(\theta)\) that will be observed on the screen where \(\theta\) is the angle shown in Fig. (1). Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c\) and \(\omega\), where \(c\) is the speed of light. Also, note that the intensity is proportional to the time average of the square of the electric field. Here you may take the proportionality constant to be \(\beta\). You may ignore the attenuation in the magnitude of the electric fields with distance from the slits to any point on the screen.
III.2. Glass slab (1.0 point)
A perfectly transparent glass slab of thickness \(w\) and refractive index \(\mu\) is introduced in the path of beam 1 before the slits. Find the expression for the intensity of the light \(I(\theta)\) that will be observed on the screen. Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c,\omega,\mu\) and \(w\).
III.3. Quarter wave plate (2.0 points)
An optical device (known as quarter wave plate (QWP)) is introduced in the path of beam 1, before the slits, replacing the glass slab. This device changes the polarization of the beam from the linear polarization state \(\vec E_1=\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t)\) to a circular polarization state which is given by
\[\vec E_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}[\hat i E_0\cos(\omega t)+\hat j E_0\sin(\omega t)].\tag{2}\]
Here \(\hat j\) is the unit vector along the y-axis. Assume that the device does not introduce any additional path difference and that it is perfectly transparent. Note that the tip of the electric field vector traces a circle as time elapses and hence, the beam is said to be circularly polarized. We assume that the angle \(\theta\) is small enough so that intensity from slit one does not depend on the angle \(\theta\) even for \(\hat j\) polarization.
III.3.a. Find the expression for the intensity \(I(\theta)\) of the light that will be observed on the screen. Express your answer in terms of \(\theta,d,E_0,c\) and \(\omega\).
III.3.b. What is the maximum intensity \(I_{\max}\)?
III.3.c. What is the minimum intensity \(I_{\min}\)?
III.4. Two polarizers (2.0 points)

Now consider the experimental setup (see Fig. (2)) in which beam 1 is subjected to the device (QWP) described in part 3 and a linear polarizer (marked as I), between \(z=a\) and \(z=b\), which allows only the component of the electric field parallel to an axis \(\hat i'\) to pass through. The unit vector \(\hat i'\) is defined as
\[\hat i'=\hat i\cos\gamma+\hat j\sin\gamma.\]
Another linear polarizer (marked as II) between \(z=b\) and \(z=c\) polarizes the beam back to \(\hat i\) direction. Thus beam 1 is back to its original state of polarization. Assume that the polarizers do not introduce any path difference and are perfectly transparent.
III.4.a. Write down the expression for the electric field of beam 1 after the first polarizer at \(z=b\), \(\vec E_1(z=b)\).
III.4.b. Write down the expression for the electric field of beam 1 after the second polarizer at \(z=c\), \(\vec E_1(z=c)\).
III.4.c. What is the phase difference \(\alpha\) between the two beams at the slits?
The most general type of polarization is elliptical polarization. A convenient way of expressing elliptical polarization is to consider it as a superposition of two orthogonal linearly polarized components, i.e.
\[\vec E=\hat i'E_0\cos e\cos(\omega t)+\hat j'E_0\sin e\sin(\omega t),\tag{3}\]
where \(\hat i'\) and \(\hat j'\) and this state of polarization are depicted in Fig. 3.

The tip of the electric field vector traces an ellipse as time elapses. Here \(e\) represents the ellipticity and is given by \(\tan e=\text{Semi-minor axis of the ellipse}/\text{Semi-major axis of the ellipse}\).
Linear polarization (Eqs. (1)) and circular polarization (Eq. (2)) are special cases of elliptical polarization (Eq. (3)). The two parameters \(\gamma\in[0,\pi]\) and \(e\in[-\pi/4,\pi/4]\) completely describe the state of polarization.
The polarization state can also be represented by a point on a sphere of unit radius called the Poincare sphere. The polarization of the beam described in Eq. (3) is represented by a point \(P\) on the Poincare sphere (see Fig. 4), then latitude \(\angle PCD=2e\) and longitude \(\angle ACD=2\gamma\). Here \(C\) is the center.

III.5. Equator (0.5 point)
Consider a point on the equator of the Poincare sphere. III.5.a. Write down the electric field \(\vec E_{\rm Eq}\) corresponding to this point. III.5.b. What is its state of polarization?
III.6. North pole (0.5 point)
Consider a point at the north pole of the Poincare sphere. III.6.a. Write down the electric field \(\vec E_{\rm NP}\) corresponding to this point. III.6.b. What is its state of polarization?
III.7. Polarization cycle (1.5 points)
Now consider the three polarization states of beam 1 as given in part 4. Let the initial polarization (at \(z=0\)) be represented by a point \(A_1\) on the Poincare sphere, after the optical device let the state (at \(z=a\)) be represented by point \(A_2\), and after the first polarizer (say, at \(z=b\)) let the state be represented by point \(A_3\). At \(z=c\), the polarization returns to its original state which is represented by \(A_1\). Locate these points (\(A_1,A_2,A_3\)) on the Poincare sphere.
III.8. Geometric phase (1.5 points)
If these three points (\(A_1,A_2,A_3\) from part (III.7)) are joined by great circles on the sphere, a triangle on the surface of the sphere is obtained. A great circle is a circle on the sphere whose center coincides with the center of the sphere. The phase difference \(\alpha\) obtained in part 4 and the area \(S\) of the curved surface enclosed by the triangle are related to each other. Relate \(S\) to \(\alpha\).
This relationship is general and was obtained by Pancharatnam and the phase difference is called the Pancharatnam phase.

Then the intensity is given by \(I(\theta)=\beta\overline{|\mathbf E_1+\mathbf E_2|^2}\). Here

\[\begin{aligned}|\mathbf E_1+\mathbf E_2|^2&=|E_0\cos(\omega t)+E_0\cos(\omega t+\delta)|^2\\&=|E_0\cos(\omega t)(1+\cos\delta)-E_0\sin(\omega t)\sin\delta|^2\\&=E_0^2[\cos^2(\omega t)(1+2\cos\delta+\cos^2\delta)+\sin^2(\omega t)\sin^2\delta\\&\qquad-2\cos(\omega t)(1+\cos\delta)\sin(\omega t)\sin\delta].\end{aligned}\]
Since \(\overline{\cos^2\omega t}=\overline{\sin^2\omega t}=1/2\) and \(\overline{\sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega t)}=0\), we get the intensity to be
The alternate derivation in the original PDF prints the following positive sine term:

\[\begin{aligned}|\mathbf E_1+\mathbf E_2|^2&=|E_0\cos(\omega t)+E_0\cos(\omega t+\delta)|^2\\&=|E_0\cos(\omega t)(1+\cos\delta)+E_0\sin(\omega t)\sin\delta|^2\\&=|E_0 A\cos(\omega t-\phi)|^2.\end{aligned}\]

Here \(A^2=(1+\cos\delta)^2+\sin^2\delta=2(1+\cos\delta)\). Since \(\overline{\cos^2(\omega t-\phi)}=1/2\), we have \(I(\theta)=(\beta/2)E_0^2A^2=\beta E_0^2(1+\cos\delta)\), where \(\delta\) is given by Eq. (1).

Thus, after taking time averages, the intensity will be
The maximum value of the intensity is \(\beta E_0^2[1+1/\sqrt2]\). The minimum value of the intensity is \(\beta E_0^2[1-1/\sqrt2]\).
The electric field at \(z=b\) is given by

\[\begin{aligned}\mathbf E_1(z=b)&=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}[\cos(\omega t-kb)\,\mathbf i\cdot\mathbf i'+\sin(\omega t-kb)\,\mathbf j\cdot\mathbf i']\,\mathbf i'\\&=\frac1{\sqrt2}[E_0\cos\gamma\cos(\omega t-kb)+E_0\sin\gamma\sin(\omega t-kb)]\,\mathbf i'\\&=\frac1{\sqrt2}[E_0\cos(\omega t-kb-\gamma)]\,\mathbf i'.\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}\mathbf E_1(z=c)&=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}[\cos(\omega t-kc-\gamma)\,\mathbf i'\cdot\mathbf i]\,\mathbf i\\&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\cos\gamma E_0\cos(\omega t-kc-\gamma)\,\mathbf i.\end{aligned}\]
Whereas \(\mathbf E_2(z=c)=E_0\cos(\omega t-kc)\,\mathbf i\). So the net phase difference between beam 1 and beam 2 is now \(\alpha=\gamma\).

Convention note: c in z=c is a position label, whereas c in the intensity formulas denotes the speed of light. The source keeps cos(gamma) as a signed amplitude when quoting alpha=gamma. For a positive-amplitude phase convention, the automatic III.4.c field is restricted to 0<gamma<pi/2. At gamma=pi/2 beam 1 is extinguished and its relative phase is undefined. Beyond that, an additional pi phase and an oriented-area convention must be considered. The source's full gamma range is retained in the statement.

solution.text:
Pancharatnam Phase
III.1. Two linearly polarized beams (1.0 mark)
Let the phase difference between two rays making an angle \(\theta\) with z direction be \(\delta\). Clearly
\[\delta=\omega\Delta t=\omega d\sin\theta/c.\tag{1}\]
Then the intensity is given by \(I(\theta)=\beta\overline{|\mathbf E_1+\mathbf E_2|^2}\). Here
\[\begin{aligned}|\mathbf E_1+\mathbf E_2|^2&=|E_0\cos(\omega t)+E_0\cos(\omega t+\delta)|^2\\&=|E_0\cos(\omega t)(1+\cos\delta)-E_0\sin(\omega t)\sin\delta|^2\\&=E_0^2[\cos^2(\omega t)(1+2\cos\delta+\cos^2\delta)+\sin^2(\omega t)\sin^2\delta\\&\qquad-2\cos(\omega t)(1+\cos\delta)\sin(\omega t)\sin\delta].\end{aligned}\]
Since \(\overline{\cos^2\omega t}=\overline{\sin^2\omega t}=1/2\) and \(\overline{\sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega t)}=0\), we get the intensity to be
\[I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2(1+\cos\delta),\]
where \(\delta\) is given by Eq. (1).
III.1. Alternate solution
The alternate derivation in the original PDF prints the following positive sine term:
\[\begin{aligned}|\mathbf E_1+\mathbf E_2|^2&=|E_0\cos(\omega t)+E_0\cos(\omega t+\delta)|^2\\&=|E_0\cos(\omega t)(1+\cos\delta)+E_0\sin(\omega t)\sin\delta|^2\\&=|E_0 A\cos(\omega t-\phi)|^2.\end{aligned}\]
Here \(A^2=(1+\cos\delta)^2+\sin^2\delta=2(1+\cos\delta)\). Since \(\overline{\cos^2(\omega t-\phi)}=1/2\), we have \(I(\theta)=(\beta/2)E_0^2A^2=\beta E_0^2(1+\cos\delta)\), where \(\delta\) is given by Eq. (1).
Source note: the alternate expansion changes the sign of the sine term compared with cos(omega t plus delta). That intermediate equality is not exact as printed. Its squared amplitude and the time-averaged intensity are unchanged. The same sign issue appears in the printed expansion in III.3 below.
III.2. Glass slab (1.0 mark)
Beam 1 has travelled extra optical path \((\mu-1)w\). Thus the net phase difference between two beams when they emerge at the angle \(\theta\) is
\[\delta=\frac\omega c[d\sin\theta-(\mu-1)w],\qquad I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2(1+\cos\delta).\]
III.3. Quarter wave plate (2.0 marks)
The two beams have travelled exactly the same paths up to the slits. Thus when they emerge at an angle \(\theta\), they have a net phase difference of \(\delta=\omega d\sin\theta/c\). The following expansion is transcribed as printed, subject to the sine-sign note above:
\[\begin{aligned}|\mathbf E_1+\mathbf E_2|^2&=\left|\mathbf i\left[\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\cos(\omega t)+E_0\cos(\omega t+\delta)\right]+\mathbf j\left[\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\sin(\omega t)\right]\right|^2\\&=\left|E_0\cos(\omega t)\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}+\cos\delta\right)+E_0\sin(\omega t)\sin\delta\right|^2+\frac{E_0^2}{2}\sin^2(\omega t)\\&=E_0^2\left[\cos^2(\omega t)\left(\frac12+\sqrt2\cos\delta+\cos^2\delta\right)+\sin^2(\omega t)\sin^2\delta\right.\\&\left.\qquad+2\cos(\omega t)\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}+\cos\delta\right)\sin(\omega t)\sin\delta\right]+\frac{E_0^2}{2}\sin^2(\omega t).\end{aligned}\]
Thus, after taking time averages, the intensity will be
\[\begin{aligned}I(\theta)&=\beta E_0^2\left[\frac12\left(\frac12+\sqrt2\cos\delta+\cos^2\delta\right)+\frac12\sin^2\delta\right]+\frac{\beta E_0^2}{4}\\&=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\frac1{\sqrt2}\cos\delta\right]=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\frac1{\sqrt2}\cos\left(\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}\right)\right].\end{aligned}\]
The maximum value of the intensity is \(\beta E_0^2[1+1/\sqrt2]\). The minimum value of the intensity is \(\beta E_0^2[1-1/\sqrt2]\).
III.4. Two polarizers (2.0 marks)
The electric field at \(z=b\) is given by
\[\begin{aligned}\mathbf E_1(z=b)&=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}[\cos(\omega t-kb)\,\mathbf i\cdot\mathbf i'+\sin(\omega t-kb)\,\mathbf j\cdot\mathbf i']\,\mathbf i'\\&=\frac1{\sqrt2}[E_0\cos\gamma\cos(\omega t-kb)+E_0\sin\gamma\sin(\omega t-kb)]\,\mathbf i'\\&=\frac1{\sqrt2}[E_0\cos(\omega t-kb-\gamma)]\,\mathbf i'.\end{aligned}\]
At \(z=c\),
\[\begin{aligned}\mathbf E_1(z=c)&=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}[\cos(\omega t-kc-\gamma)\,\mathbf i'\cdot\mathbf i]\,\mathbf i\\&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\cos\gamma E_0\cos(\omega t-kc-\gamma)\,\mathbf i.\end{aligned}\]
Whereas \(\mathbf E_2(z=c)=E_0\cos(\omega t-kc)\,\mathbf i\). So the net phase difference between beam 1 and beam 2 is now \(\alpha=\gamma\).
Convention note: c in z=c is a position label, whereas c in the intensity formulas denotes the speed of light. The source keeps cos(gamma) as a signed amplitude when quoting alpha=gamma. For a positive-amplitude phase convention, the automatic III.4.c field is restricted to 0<gamma<pi/2. At gamma=pi/2 beam 1 is extinguished and its relative phase is undefined. Beyond that, an additional pi phase and an oriented-area convention must be considered. The source's full gamma range is retained in the statement.
III.5. Equator (0.5 mark)
(a) At the equator \(e=0\). Then \(\mathbf E=\mathbf E_{\rm Eq}=\mathbf i'E_0\cos(\omega t)\). (b) Clearly the beam is linearly polarized along \(\mathbf i'\).
III.6. North pole (0.5 mark)
(a) At the north pole \(e=\pi/4\) and \(\gamma\) can be taken to be 0. Then \(\mathbf i'=\mathbf i\) and \(\mathbf j'=\mathbf j\). The electric field is
\[\mathbf E_{\rm NP}=\mathbf i\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\cos(\omega t)+\mathbf j\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\sin(\omega t).\]
(b) This represents circular polarization.
III.7. Polarization cycle (1.5 marks)

III.8. Geometric phase (1.5 marks)
From the figure it is clear that the area of the spherical triangle \(A_1A_2A_3\) is \(2\pi\times(2\gamma/(2\pi))=2\gamma\) and the phase difference was \(\gamma\). Thus the phase difference is half the area of the spherical triangle \(A_1A_2A_3\) on the Poincare sphere. Thus \(S=2\alpha\).
Here beam 1 passes through various states of polarization and returns to its original state. Though there has been no additional path difference, the beam has picked up a phase \(\gamma\) with respect to beam 2. This is called the Pancharatnam phase.
The III.8 answer field uses the source's positive-area branch, with 0<alpha<pi/2. Vector expressions, polarization descriptions and the sphere construction are retained as self-review responses rather than being reduced to an automatic scalar check.

solution.text:
T1: Sunny
a. Reflected illuminance
The nearby A and B readings compare direct sunlight with shadow, so \(I_0\) is the direct-sun illuminance surplus. Let a ray hit the cylinder at a horizontal normal-incidence angle \(\alpha\), and let \(l\) be its horizontal travel distance after reflection. Define \(\beta=\pi-\alpha\). Specular reflection changes the horizontal direction by twice the incidence angle.


An incident strip of width \(dx\) maps into a floor strip of azimuthal width \(2l\,d\alpha\). The vertical-to-floor-distance mapping is the same for the direct and reflected ray, so that factor cancels in power conservation:
\[I_0\,dx=2Il\,d\alpha,\qquad |dx|=a\cos\alpha\,|d\alpha|,\qquad I=\frac{I_0a\cos\alpha}{2l}.\]
To leading order in \(a/r\), \(l\simeq r\) and \(\theta\simeq\pi-2\alpha\). Thus \(\cos\alpha=\sin(\theta/2)\) and
\[I(r,\theta)\simeq\frac{I_0a}{2r}\sin\frac\theta2.\]
Use the full polar angle around the illuminated side, \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\), so the sine is nonnegative. Finite-cylinder corrections are beyond the requested leading far-field approximation. The source also writes the intermediate refinement \(I=-I_0a\cos\beta/\sqrt{4l^2+a^2\sin^2\beta}\), which has the same leading term.
b. Ring position
Approximate the middle blocking finger as horizontal. In the side-view construction the reflected horizontal distance satisfies \(l=l_0+a\cos\alpha\). At grazing incidence \(\alpha=\pi/2\), \(R_{\min}\simeq l_0\). The triangle joining cylinder centre, reflection point and floor point gives
\[r^2=a^2+l^2-2al\cos\beta=a^2+l^2+2al\cos\alpha.\]
Substitute \(l\simeq R_{\min}+a\cos\alpha\) and keep terms through first order in \(a/R_{\min}\). Then \(r^2\simeq R_{\min}^2+4aR_{\min}\cos\alpha\), so
\[R(\theta)-R_{\min}\simeq2a\cos\alpha=2a\sin\frac\theta2.\]
Both the change in the reflected path length and the offset of the reflection point contribute. Dropping either loses the factor of two. The original examiner marking tables remain in the solution PDF.

solution.text:
T2: Floating table
a. Equilibrium forces and stability
Treat each pair of chains as one chain with the combined tension. Let \(C\) be the uniform plate's centre of mass, \(A\) the movable short-chain attachment, and \(B\) the movable long-chain attachment. The diagram gives horizontal lever arms \(BC=4a\), \(BA=2a\), short-chain length \(4a\), and long-chain length \(6a\).

\[F_1-F_2-mg=0,\qquad 4amg-2aF_1=0,\qquad F_1=2mg,\quad F_2=mg.\]
Both tensions are positive. To check stability one must also account for the constraints. A small horizontal displacement \(x\) cannot produce first-order rotation: both chain attachments initially move horizontally and rigid-body length constraints make their first-order velocities equal. The tilt and vertical centre displacement are of order \(x^2\). Both chain forces then acquire horizontal components opposite to \(x\).

\[F_x\simeq-F_1\frac{x}{4a}-F_2\frac{x}{6a}=-\frac{2mg}{3a}x.\]
This restoring force proves stable equilibrium, with tension maintained for sufficiently small oscillations.
b. Small-oscillation period
\[\ddot x+\frac{2g}{3a}x=0,\qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{3a}{2g}}=0.777\,\mathrm s.\]
Alternative: constraint geometry and energy

Let the centre shift by \((x,y)\), and let \(\varphi\) be the small clockwise tilt. To the order needed, short- and long-chain length conservation gives
\[x^2-8a(y-2a\varphi)=0,\qquad x^2+12a(y-4a\varphi)=0.\]
\[y=\frac{x^2}{3a},\qquad\varphi=\frac{5x^2}{48a^2},\qquad U=\frac{mgx^2}{3a},\qquad K\simeq\frac12m\dot x^2.\]
The positive quadratic potential establishes stability independently. Since \(y\) and \(\varphi\) are second order in \(x\), their kinetic-energy contributions are higher order. The energy equation gives the same period.
Alternative: trajectory curvature


At equilibrium the instantaneous angular velocity vanishes and every point has speed \(v\). The centre-path curvature is then linear in horizontal coordinate. At \(B\) it is \(-1/(6a)\), and at \(A\), \(1/(4a)\). Extrapolating from their horizontal positions, \(x_B=4a\), \(x_A=2a\), gives centre curvature \(2/(3a)\), or radius \(R_C=3a/2\). Therefore \(T=2\pi\sqrt{R_C/g}\). Equivalently the normal-acceleration construction gives \(w_C=w_B+2w_{Ay}=v^2/(6a)+2v^2/(4a)=v^2/(3a/2)\). Original construction diagrams and marking details remain in the PDF.

solution.text:
T3: Crossed wires
a. Helical field line
The wire's field is circular, with magnitude \(\mu_0I/(2\pi\rho)\). Adding a constant axial field makes each field line a helix centred on the wire. Its handedness follows the right-hand rule for the current and the sign of the applied axial field. It is smooth, not closed, and has constant pitch at fixed radius.

b. Conserved flux tube
Near wire \(X\), its azimuthal field dominates, so the combined field line is a tightly wound spiral of slowly varying radius \(\rho(x)\). Consider the surface formed by all field lines through the radius-\(r\) circle at \(x=3a\). This is a flux tube. Its sides are tangent to the field, so no flux leaves them. The cross-sections are nearly circular because \(\rho\ll\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\).

The axial field comes from wire \(Y\): \(B_\parallel=(\mu_0I/2\pi)a/(a^2+x^2)\). It is approximately uniform across each small tube section. Conserved flux gives
\[B_\parallel\pi\rho^2=\frac{\mu_0Ia\rho^2}{2(a^2+x^2)}=\mathrm{const},\qquad\frac{\rho(x)^2}{a^2+x^2}=\frac{r^2}{10a^2}.\]
\[\rho(x)=\frac r{\sqrt{10}}\sqrt{1+\frac{x^2}{a^2}},\qquad d=\rho(0)=\frac r{\sqrt{10}}.\]
The validity ratio \(\rho/\sqrt{a^2+x^2}=r/(\sqrt{10}a)\) is constant and small along the whole tube.
c. Field-line length

To leading order the field-line tangent satisfies \(dx/dL\simeq B_\parallel/B_\perp\), with \(B_\perp\simeq\mu_0I/(2\pi\rho)\). The precise angular position of closest approach is negligible compared with the long tightly wound path. Hence
\[L\simeq\int_0^{3a}\frac{a^2+x^2}{a\rho(x)}\,dx=\frac{\sqrt{10}a^2}{r}\int_0^3\sqrt{1+u^2}\,du.\]
A single trapezoid gives the integral \(3(1+\sqrt{10})/2\simeq6.24\), yielding \(L\simeq197\,\mathrm m\), within the requested accuracy. Exact integration, for example using \(u=\sinh\beta\), gives
\[\int_0^3\sqrt{1+u^2}\,du=\frac12\left[3\sqrt{10}+\ln(3+\sqrt{10})\right]\simeq5.65,\]
\[L\simeq17.9\frac{a^2}{r}\simeq179\,\mathrm m.\]
The numeric field allows the requested 20 percent estimate, including the trapezoid result. The helix sketch remains self-review. Full source marking tables remain in the PDF.

solution.text:
T1: Sliding puck
a. Sliding followed by possible rolling
The wall normal force supplies centripetal acceleration, \(N=Mv^2/R\), to leading order in \(r/R\). Friction \(F=\mu Mv^2/R\) decreases the translation speed and spins the puck with moment of inertia \(I=Mr^2/2\).

\[\dot v=-\frac\mu Rv^2,\qquad r\dot\omega=\frac{2\mu}{R}v^2,\qquad v(0)=v_0,\quad\omega(0)=0.\]
Define \(\tau=R/(\mu v_0)\). Integrating while contact slips gives
\[v(t)=\frac{v_0}{1+t/\tau},\qquad r\omega(t)=\frac{2v_0(t/\tau)}{1+t/\tau}.\]

Rolling begins when \(v=r\omega\), at \(t_1=\tau/2\) and \(v_1=2v_0/3\). No tangential friction is needed afterward, since the normal force acts through the centre. Integration of distance gives \(l=v_0\tau\ln(1+t/\tau)\). At the wall end \(l=\pi R\), so the hypothetical sliding-exit time is \(t_e=\tau(e^{\pi\mu}-1)\). Compare it with \(t_1\):
\[\mu_c=\frac{\ln(3/2)}\pi,\qquad v_e=\begin{cases}v_0e^{-\pi\mu},&0\le\mu\le\mu_c,\\2v_0/3,&\mu\ge\mu_c.\end{cases}\]
Alternative: integrate in turning angle
Using \(dl=R\,d\varphi=v\,dt\), the same equations give \(dv/v=-\mu\,d\varphi\). Hence \(v(\varphi)=v_0e^{-\mu\varphi}\) and \(r\omega=2v_0(1-e^{-\mu\varphi})\). The rolling condition occurs at \(\mu\varphi_c=\ln(3/2)\). Comparing \(\varphi_c\) with \(\pi\) reproduces the two branches. This argument also works for other smooth wall shapes with the same total turning angle, to leading order in puck size.

Each sends gifts to the other at regular intervals \(\Delta t_0\) measured in their own frame, with gift speed \(v=4c/5\) in that frame. Their separation \(L\) is large enough that many gifts are in transit at once.
In Bob's frame, find the distance between successive gifts sent by Alice.
Find the interval \(\Delta t_1\) at which Alice's gifts arrive at Bob.
At one instant Alice sees gifts moving away from her and gifts moving towards her. Find the ratio of these two numbers.

statement.text:
T2: Spaceships
Alice and Bob are twin astronauts approaching each other to reunite. Alice's spaceship moves towards Bob at \(u=3c/5\), where \(c\) is light speed. Each sends gifts to the other at regular intervals \(\Delta t_0\) measured in their own frame, with gift speed \(v=4c/5\) in that frame. Their separation \(L\) is large enough that many gifts are in transit at once.
a.i
In Bob's frame, find the distance between successive gifts sent by Alice.
a.ii
Find the interval \(\Delta t_1\) at which Alice's gifts arrive at Bob.
b
At one instant Alice sees gifts moving away from her and gifts moving towards her. Find the ratio of these two numbers.

solution.text:
T2: Spaceships
a.i. Simultaneous separation in Bob's frame
Relativistic velocity addition gives gift speed \(w=(u+v)/(1+uv/c^2)=35c/37\) in the receiving frame. Successive emission events occur at the same place in Alice's frame, so Bob measures their interval as \(\gamma_u\Delta t_0\), with \(\gamma_u=5/4\). During that interval Alice moves by \(u\gamma_u\Delta t_0\), while the first gift travels \(w\gamma_u\Delta t_0\). Their simultaneous separation is
\[l_B=(w-u)\gamma_u\Delta t_0=\frac{16}{37}c\Delta t_0.\]

Alternatively, the spacing in Alice's frame is \(l_A=v\Delta t_0\). Boosting first to the gifts' rest frame gives proper spacing \(l_G=\gamma_vl_A\); boosting to Bob gives \(l_B=l_G/\gamma_w\). Here \(\gamma_v=5/3\), \(\gamma_w=37/12\), so the same \(16c\Delta t_0/37\) follows.
a.ii. Arrival interval
\[\Delta t_1=\frac{l_B}{w}=\frac{16}{35}\Delta t_0.\]
One may find the arrival interval first by intersecting successive gift worldlines with Bob's worldline and transforming the two arrival events. Their separation is at one place in Bob's frame, unlike the two emission events.

b. Gifts actually seen
Seeing is not a simultaneous inventory. Count the gift worldlines intersecting Alice's past light cone. Suppose Bob appears at distance \(d_B\) and lookback time \(t_l=d_B/c\). The oldest outgoing gift Alice still sees has apparent distance \(d_B+vt_l\). The newest visible incoming gift has apparent distance \(d_B-wt_l\). Therefore
\[N_\mathrm{out}\simeq\frac{d_B(1+v/c)}{v\Delta t_0},\qquad N_\mathrm{in}\simeq\frac{d_B(1-w/c)}{l_B},\]
\[\frac{N_\mathrm{out}}{N_\mathrm{in}}=\frac{1+v/c}{1-w/c}\frac{l_B}{v\Delta t_0}=18.\]
The large number of gifts makes endpoint and integer-count effects negligible. By symmetry the calculation can equally be done using Bob as observer.


Graphical and imaginary-time alternatives

With \(c=\Delta t_0=1\), Lorentz diagrams also give simultaneous spacing \(16/37\) and reception interval \(16/35\). The corresponding Alice-frame intersection coordinates are \((20/37,-12/37)\) for simultaneous Bob time and \((12/35,-20/35)\) for arrival. Applying \(t_B=(5/4)(t_A+3x_A/5)\), or the invariant interval, gives the same results.


In the source's \(ict\) construction, \(\tan\alpha=-3i/5\), \(\tan\beta=-4i/5\), and \(\tan\gamma=-35i/37\). The sine rule gives the same spacings and intervals. For the visible count, the construction gives \(AP=(9/2)il\) and \(RQ=(1/4)il\), whose ratio is 18. A source intermediate spacing formula is labelled as a time interval, and one printed count-ratio denominator uses \(c-v\) instead of \(c-w\). The results above use the consistent event and velocity definitions. All original approaches and marking details remain in the PDF.

statement.text:

Two identical parallel planar mirrors are separated by \(L\), with air inside and outside. They are symmetric under illumination from either side, lossless and partially reflecting. At normal incidence the reflected intensity is \(R\) times the incident intensity, where \(0<R<1\) and \(1-R\ll1\). A monochromatic laser of power \(P\) enters normally.
