solution.text:
T3: Fabry–Pérot interferometer
a and b. Complex amplitudes
Let \(r\) and \(t\) be amplitude reflection and transmission coefficients, with \(|r|^2=R\), \(|t|^2=1-R\). Write \(A\) for the incoming amplitude, \(B,C\) for the forward and backward intracavity waves at the first mirror, and \(D\) for the outgoing amplitude. Boundary conditions are
\[B=tA+rC,\qquad 0=rA+tC,\qquad D=tB,\qquad C=rBe^{2ikL}.\]
Eliminating amplitudes gives \(e^{-2ikL}=r^2-t^2\), hence \(|r^2-t^2|=1\). Losslessness gives \(|r|^2+|t|^2=1\). Equality in the complex triangle inequality requires \(r^2\) and \(-t^2\) to have the same phase. Thus
\[\operatorname{Re}(rt^*)=0,\qquad \phi=\arg t-\arg r=\pm\frac\pi2\pmod\pi,\qquad |\phi|=\frac\pi2.\]
This is the reflected-transmitted relative phase, as defined explicitly in the official solution. A common phase on both coefficients is not determined. The statement's wording about transmission alone needs this qualification. Some intermediate conjugate algebra in the source has incorrect signs, but its phase result follows from the triangle argument above.
Alternative: sum the reflected paths
\[A_\mathrm{back}=rA\left[1+\frac{t^2e^{2ikL}}{1-r^2e^{2ikL}}\right]=0.\]
The direct reflection and all multiply reflected transmitted paths form a geometric series. Its zero gives the same resonance equation and relative phase.
c. Stored energy and returning pulse
The initial forward intracavity power is \(P/(1-R)\), and the backward power is \(RP/(1-R)\). The stored energy is \(U=(1+R)LP/[c(1-R)]\), approximately \(2LP/[c(1-R)]\). At high reflectivity the release is almost symmetric, so the returning energy is approximately half of \(U\):
\[E_\mathrm{back}\simeq\frac{LP}{c(1-R)}.\]
The exact ideal abrupt-switch calculation clarifies the approximation. Once the incident wave disappears at the first mirror, the returning amplitude begins at \(-rA\). It is multiplied by \(r^2e^{2ikL}\) every round trip \(\Delta=2L/c\), so the returning powers are \(PR,PR^3,PR^5,\ldots\). Summing their energies gives
\[E_\mathrm{back}=\frac{2LPR}{c(1-R^2)}\simeq\frac{LP}{c(1-R)}.\]
The printed source series skips a power in one term. The exact geometric series above uses successive odd powers of the intensity reflectivity. The answer field requests the leading high-reflectivity result stated in the problem.
d. Pulse duration
The energy envelope decays as \(R^{2t/\Delta}\). Its time constant is
\[\tau_E=\frac{L}{c\ln(1/R)}\simeq\frac{L}{c(1-R)}.\]
The same estimate follows from \(-\dot U\simeq2P\), the energy escaping through both mirrors. Pulse duration is an estimate, and amplitude-decay time differs by a factor of two from the energy-decay time. The field explicitly checks the leading energy-envelope time constant, while other stated duration conventions require self-review.
Additional source approaches

If one additionally models each mirror as an ideal sheet with continuous electric field, \(1+r=t\). Together with losslessness, the complex coefficient triangle again makes \(r\) and \(t\) perpendicular. This continuity model is an extra assumption, not needed for the general result.



A real-amplitude energy argument superposes those two illumination cases so the leftward outputs cancel. Equal total incoming and outgoing power requires \(\cos[2(\theta-\psi)]=-1\), hence the same quarter-cycle phase. The source's corresponding cosine equation has a typo. Its full original derivations and marking tables remain in the reference PDF.

statement.text:
T1: Thermal lens
An intense laser beam incident on a semitransparent plate can self-focus behind it because inhomogeneous heating changes the refractive index. Consider material with positive thermo-optic coefficient \(\gamma=dn/dT\).
A semitransparent disk has radius \(a=15.0\,\mathrm{mm}\), thickness \(b=0.2\,\mathrm{mm}\), optical absorption coefficient \(A=0.1\), thermal conductivity \(k=0.3\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}K^{-1}}\), and \(\gamma=2.5\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}\). Its outer rim is thermally connected to a circular metallic holder maintained at \(T_h=20^\circ\mathrm C\). A parallel laser beam of radius \(\sigma=0.5\,\mathrm{mm}\) and power \(P_L=20\,\mathrm{mW}\) falls normally on the disk centre, with uniform intensity across its cross-section.

a
Sketch the qualitative temperature profile \(T(r)\), where \(r\) is distance from the beam axis. Clearly mark the illuminated region \(0\le r\le\sigma\) and outer region \(\sigma\le r\le a\).
b
Near the centre, \(T(r)=T_c+mr^2\). Calculate \(T_c\) and \(m\).
c
Show that the beam focuses at one point and find its distance \(f\) from the disk. If you did not find \(T_c\) and \(m\), you may use them as parameters in the final answer.
Ignore thermal expansion, radiation and heat exchange with the air. Take the refractive index of air as \(n_{\rm air}=1\).

children.text: The profile has a horizontal tangent at \(r=0\), is decreasing and concave down within the beam, decreasing and convex outside it, and reaches \(T_h\) with a nonzero negative slope at \(a\). Temperature and slope match at \(r=\sigma\).

children.text: At steady state, the absorbed power inside radius \(r\) flows out through area \(2\pi rb\). The supplied \(A\) is the dimensionless absorbed fraction, so
\[-2\pi kbr\frac{dT}{dr}=P_{\rm abs}(r),\qquad P_{\rm abs}(r)=\begin{cases}AP_Lr^2/\sigma^2,&0\le r\le\sigma,\\ AP_L,&\sigma\le r\le a.\end{cases}\]
Integrating inside and outside, with \(T(0)=T_c\) and \(T(a)=T_h\), gives
\[T(r)=\begin{cases}T_c-\dfrac{AP_Lr^2}{4\pi kb\sigma^2},&0\le r\le\sigma,\\ T_h+\dfrac{AP_L}{2\pi kb}\ln\dfrac ar,&\sigma\le r\le a.\end{cases}\]

An alternative is to substitute the quadratic form directly into the heat-flow equation to get \(m\), and integrate \(T_c-T_h=\int_0^a P_{\rm abs}(r)/(2\pi kbr)\,dr\) piecewise to get the same central temperature. The source's intermediate absorbed-power equation omits \(A\) in one expression for the incident intensity. The consistent absorbed power includes \(A\), as above. Its marking-table match point should read \(r=\sigma\), not \(a\).

solution.text:
T1: Thermal lens
a. Temperature profile
The profile has a horizontal tangent at \(r=0\), is decreasing and concave down within the beam, decreasing and convex outside it, and reaches \(T_h\) with a nonzero negative slope at \(a\). Temperature and slope match at \(r=\sigma\).

b. Radial heat flow
At steady state, the absorbed power inside radius \(r\) flows out through area \(2\pi rb\). The supplied \(A\) is the dimensionless absorbed fraction, so
\[-2\pi kbr\frac{dT}{dr}=P_{\rm abs}(r),\qquad P_{\rm abs}(r)=\begin{cases}AP_Lr^2/\sigma^2,&0\le r\le\sigma,\\ AP_L,&\sigma\le r\le a.\end{cases}\]
Integrating inside and outside, with \(T(0)=T_c\) and \(T(a)=T_h\), gives
\[T(r)=\begin{cases}T_c-\dfrac{AP_Lr^2}{4\pi kb\sigma^2},&0\le r\le\sigma,\\ T_h+\dfrac{AP_L}{2\pi kb}\ln\dfrac ar,&\sigma\le r\le a.\end{cases}\]
\[m=-\frac{AP_L}{4\pi kb\sigma^2}\simeq-1.06\times10^7\,\mathrm{K/m^2}.\]
Matching the temperatures at \(\sigma\) yields
\[T_c=T_h+\frac{AP_L}{4\pi kb}\left[1+2\ln\left(\frac a\sigma\right)\right]\simeq40.7^\circ\mathrm C\simeq41^\circ\mathrm C.\]
An alternative is to substitute the quadratic form directly into the heat-flow equation to get \(m\), and integrate \(T_c-T_h=\int_0^a P_{\rm abs}(r)/(2\pi kbr)\,dr\) piecewise to get the same central temperature. The source's intermediate absorbed-power equation omits \(A\) in one expression for the incident intensity. The consistent absorbed power includes \(A\), as above. Its marking-table match point should read \(r=\sigma\), not \(a\).
c. Fermat's principle

Within the beam, \(n(0)-n(r)=\gamma|m|r^2\). In a thin plate rays travel approximately the same distance \(b\) inside the material and exit at nearly their entrance radius. The optical path to a focus at distance \(f\gg r\) is
\[s(r)\simeq bn(r)+\sqrt{f^2+r^2}\simeq bn(r)+f+\frac{r^2}{2f}.\]
A common focus requires this path to be independent of \(r\). Equivalently \(b[n(0)-n(r)]=r^2/(2f)\), or \(bn'(r)+r/f=0\). Since the index difference is quadratic, the same \(f\) works for every illuminated radius:
\[f=\frac1{2\gamma b|m|}=\frac{2\pi k\sigma^2}{\gamma AP_L}\simeq0.94\,\mathrm m.\]
Alternative: ray and wavefront tracing
Approximate a ray inside the disk by a circular arc with local radius \(R=-n/n'\). Snell's law between nearby radii gives internal bending \(\varphi\simeq-bn'/n\). Refraction into air gives \(\theta\simeq n\varphi=-bn'=2\gamma|m|br\). Thus \(f\simeq r/\theta=1/(2\gamma b|m|)\). The factor \(b\) is absent from one intermediate angle equation in the source, but is necessary dimensionally and agrees with its final focal length.

Alternatively, the wavefront angular speed is \(\dot\varphi=d(c/n)/dr=-cn'/n^2\), and travel time is \(bn/c\), giving the same \(\varphi=-bn'/n\). A more explicit path calculation uses \(n(r)\cos\varphi=n(r_0)\). Expanding near entrance radius \(r_0\) gives
\[-\frac{dr}{dx}\simeq\sqrt{\frac{4\gamma|m|r_0}{n(r_0)}}\sqrt{r_0-r},\qquad r(x)\simeq r_0-\frac{\gamma|m|r_0}{n(r_0)}x^2.\]
The exit angle inside the disk is \(-r'(b)\simeq2\gamma|m|r_0b/n(r_0)\). Refraction into air again gives \(\theta\simeq2\gamma|m|r_0b\), proving the same common focal point to the stated paraxial accuracy. Original partial-credit tables for all approaches are retained in the solution PDF.

children.text: A small brick is squeezed between two parallel planes in zero gravity. The planes are perpendicular to the \(z\)-axis. The lower plane moves at constant velocity \(u_1\) along \(x\), and the upper plane at constant velocity \(u_2\) along \(y\). Initially the brick is at rest. Its kinetic friction coefficient with each plane is identical.

nodes.alt: Original apparatus: a brick between parallel planes perpendicular to z, with lower plane velocity u1 along x and upper plane velocity u2 along y.

children.text: Find the brick's speed \(v_\infty\) after a long time for \(u_1=u_2\).

statement.text:
T2: Brick between two planes
A small brick is squeezed between two parallel planes in zero gravity. The planes are perpendicular to the \(z\)-axis. The lower plane moves at constant velocity \(u_1\) along \(x\), and the upper plane at constant velocity \(u_2\) along \(y\). Initially the brick is at rest. Its kinetic friction coefficient with each plane is identical.

a
Find the brick's speed \(v_\infty\) after a long time for \(u_1=u_2\).
b
Find \(v_\infty\) for \(u_1\ne u_2\).

children.text: Vertical force balance makes the normal forces equal. The friction forces therefore have equal magnitudes \(F\), and each points along the corresponding plane's velocity relative to the brick. Their resultant bisects the angle between the relative-velocity vectors. When \(u_1=u_2=u\), symmetry keeps the brick velocity along the diagonal. At steady state the two relative velocities are opposite. Hence \(v_x=v_y=u/2\), giving

nodes.alt: Original equal-speed velocity triangle: the final brick velocity v meets the line joining the two perpendicular plane velocities, and the two opposite relative velocities have equal length.

children.text: Let \(s_1=|\mathbf u_1-\mathbf v|\), \(s_2=|\mathbf u_2-\mathbf v|\), and let \(\psi\) be the angle between these relative velocities. Newton's law gives \(\dot s_1=\dot s_2=-(F/m)(1+\cos\psi)\). Thus \(s_1-s_2\) is conserved, with initial value \(\delta=u_1-u_2\).

At steady state the relative velocities are antiparallel. Their sum of lengths is \(D=|\mathbf u_1-\mathbf u_2|=\sqrt{u_1^2+u_2^2}\). Therefore \(s_1=(D+\delta)/2\), \(s_2=(D-\delta)/2\). The final velocity lies on the segment joining \(\mathbf u_1\) and \(\mathbf u_2\):

nodes.alt: Original unequal-speed velocity triangle, showing opposite final relative velocities u1-prime and u2-prime along the segment joining u1 and u2, with brick velocity v from the origin.

children.text: An equivalent form in the source is \(v_\infty=\frac1{\sqrt2}\sqrt{u_1u_2-(u_1-u_2)^2[(u_1+u_2)/D-1]}\). The component form above is less susceptible to cancellation when the plane speeds differ greatly.

Differentiating \(s_1^2=(u_1-v_x)^2+v_y^2\) and \(s_2^2=v_x^2+(u_2-v_y)^2\) recovers the same invariant \(s_1-s_2\). Setting both accelerations to zero gives \(u_1u_2=u_1v_y+u_2v_x\), which describes the same velocity segment. Together these determine the result. Equal friction magnitudes do not imply equal relative speeds. The source's diagrams of deliberately incorrect approaches are not answer diagrams. Its full marking schemes remain in the PDF.

solution.text:
T2: Brick between two planes
a. Equal speeds
Vertical force balance makes the normal forces equal. The friction forces therefore have equal magnitudes \(F\), and each points along the corresponding plane's velocity relative to the brick. Their resultant bisects the angle between the relative-velocity vectors. When \(u_1=u_2=u\), symmetry keeps the brick velocity along the diagonal. At steady state the two relative velocities are opposite. Hence \(v_x=v_y=u/2\), giving
\[v_\infty=\frac{u}{\sqrt2}.\]

b. Unequal speeds
Let \(s_1=|\mathbf u_1-\mathbf v|\), \(s_2=|\mathbf u_2-\mathbf v|\), and let \(\psi\) be the angle between these relative velocities. Newton's law gives \(\dot s_1=\dot s_2=-(F/m)(1+\cos\psi)\). Thus \(s_1-s_2\) is conserved, with initial value \(\delta=u_1-u_2\).
At steady state the relative velocities are antiparallel. Their sum of lengths is \(D=|\mathbf u_1-\mathbf u_2|=\sqrt{u_1^2+u_2^2}\). Therefore \(s_1=(D+\delta)/2\), \(s_2=(D-\delta)/2\). The final velocity lies on the segment joining \(\mathbf u_1\) and \(\mathbf u_2\):

\[v_x=\frac{u_1}{2}\left(1-\frac\delta D\right),\qquad v_y=\frac{u_2}{2}\left(1+\frac\delta D\right),\]
\[v_\infty=\frac12\sqrt{u_1^2\left(1-\frac\delta D\right)^2+u_2^2\left(1+\frac\delta D\right)^2}.\]
An equivalent form in the source is \(v_\infty=\frac1{\sqrt2}\sqrt{u_1u_2-(u_1-u_2)^2[(u_1+u_2)/D-1]}\). The component form above is less susceptible to cancellation when the plane speeds differ greatly.
Alternative: Cartesian equations
\[\dot v_x=\frac Fm\left(\frac{u_1-v_x}{s_1}-\frac{v_x}{s_2}\right),\qquad \dot v_y=\frac Fm\left(-\frac{v_y}{s_1}+\frac{u_2-v_y}{s_2}\right).\]
Differentiating \(s_1^2=(u_1-v_x)^2+v_y^2\) and \(s_2^2=v_x^2+(u_2-v_y)^2\) recovers the same invariant \(s_1-s_2\). Setting both accelerations to zero gives \(u_1u_2=u_1v_y+u_2v_x\), which describes the same velocity segment. Together these determine the result. Equal friction magnitudes do not imply equal relative speeds. The source's diagrams of deliberately incorrect approaches are not answer diagrams. Its full marking schemes remain in the PDF.

children.text: Two identical long cylindrical rod magnets of radius \(R\) share a vertical symmetry axis and have the same polarity orientation. Their narrow air gap has uniform magnetic field \(\mathbf B=B\hat{\mathbf z}\). The field outside the gap is zero. A large horizontal non-magnetic metal plate is placed in the gap and moved at constant velocity \(v\hat{\mathbf y}\). Its thickness is \(\delta\) and resistivity \(\varrho\).

statement.text:
T3: Plate between magnets
Two identical long cylindrical rod magnets of radius \(R\) share a vertical symmetry axis and have the same polarity orientation. Their narrow air gap has uniform magnetic field \(\mathbf B=B\hat{\mathbf z}\). The field outside the gap is zero. A large horizontal non-magnetic metal plate is placed in the gap and moved at constant velocity \(v\hat{\mathbf y}\). Its thickness is \(\delta\) and resistivity \(\varrho\).

a
Sketch the current streamlines in the plate at a given time, and indicate the axes.
b
Find and plot the current density along the line parallel to \(y\) through the magnets' symmetry axis.
c
Find the horizontal force required to move the plate.

children.text: The conventional motional current points along \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B=+vB\hat{\mathbf x}\). Charges accumulate near the circular field boundary until the current is divergence-free. Ohm's law is \(\mathbf j=(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)/\varrho\). The electrostatic field persists outside the magnetic patch, where currents return and close the loops. Streamlines are continuous, do not intersect, and kink at the circular boundary because their tangential component can jump.

nodes.alt: Original current streamlines inside and outside the circular magnetic patch. Axes place positive x downwards and positive y rightwards. Current flows along positive x inside and returns outside in symmetric loops.

children.text: Model the electric field as that of a uniformly polarized cylinder with polarization vector \(\mathbf P\). This field is obtained by superposing two slightly displaced oppositely charged cylinders with \(q\mathbf s=-\mathbf P\), then taking their displacement to zero. Gauss's law gives \(\mathbf E_\mathrm{in}=-\mathbf P/(2\epsilon_0)\), and outside, for planar radius vector \(\mathbf r\),

nodes.alt: Original construction using two oppositely charged overlapping cylinders with displacement s and the resulting polarized-cylinder field, including uniform inner field and dipole-like outer field.

children.text: Match the normal current across \(r=R\). The polarization surface charge \(\sigma=\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}\) must cancel the discontinuity in the normal motional current. This gives \(\mathbf P=\epsilon_0\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\). Therefore
\[\mathbf j_\mathrm{in}=\frac{\mathbf v\times\mathbf B}{2\varrho},\qquad \mathbf j_\mathrm{out}=\frac{R^2}{2\varrho r^4}\left[r^2\mathbf v-2\mathbf r(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v)\right]\times\mathbf B.\]
On the requested line \(x=0\), only \(j_x\) is nonzero:

nodes.alt: Original graph of jx against y: constant positive vB/(2 rho) between minus R and R, a jump to minus vB/(2 rho) just outside both rims, and negative inverse-square tails tending to zero.

children.text: The ideal sharp field boundary permits the tangential-current jumps at the two rims. The inside and outside answer fields specify their open domains.
Only current inside the magnetic patch experiences magnetic force. It is uniform, so integrate \(d\mathbf F=\mathbf j\times\mathbf B\,dV\) over volume \(\pi R^2\delta\):
\[\mathbf F_\mathrm{mag}=-\frac{\pi R^2\delta B^2}{2\varrho}\mathbf v,\qquad \mathbf F_\mathrm{pull}=\frac{\pi R^2\delta B^2v}{2\varrho}\hat{\mathbf y}.\]

Alternatively integrate Joule heating. Inside, \(P_\mathrm{in}=\varrho j_\mathrm{in}^2\pi R^2\delta=\pi R^2\delta v^2B^2/(4\varrho)\). Outside, \(j_\mathrm{out}^2=R^4v^2B^2/(4\varrho^2r^4)\), and integrating over annuli gives the same power. Thus \(F_\mathrm{pull}v=P_\mathrm{in}+P_\mathrm{out}\), confirming the force.

The source's current-conservation condition is written with a cross-product loop integral. The intended condition is \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf j=0\), equivalently zero net normal flux through a closed boundary. A separate circulation condition applies to the electric field. Several intermediate signs and dimensional factors in the source are typographical. The final currents and force above satisfy both boundary conditions.

The source also discusses a stepping-magnet Faraday model that happens to reproduce the in-plane current formulas but gives an incorrect electric field away from the plate. It is not a valid derivation of that three-dimensional field. In a correctly transformed continuously moving magnet, surface-charge fields cancel the external induced field. The streamlines outside the patch are circles tangent to the boundary: their tangency follows from \(2\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf r=r^2\), with \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf P=0\).

nodes.alt: Original outer-current geometry: family of circular streamlines, a chosen circle centre a, point r, its tangent current vector and radial vector r minus a.

children.text: The assumed current is uniform through the plate thickness. Magnetic diffusion has diffusivity \(\varrho/\mu_0\), and the passage time is of order \(R/v\). Skin depth much greater than \(\delta\) requires \(\varrho R\gg\mu_0v\delta^2\). solution.text:
T3: Plate between magnets
a. Steady current pattern
The conventional motional current points along \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B=+vB\hat{\mathbf x}\). Charges accumulate near the circular field boundary until the current is divergence-free. Ohm's law is \(\mathbf j=(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)/\varrho\). The electrostatic field persists outside the magnetic patch, where currents return and close the loops. Streamlines are continuous, do not intersect, and kink at the circular boundary because their tangential component can jump.

b. Polarized-cylinder construction
Model the electric field as that of a uniformly polarized cylinder with polarization vector \(\mathbf P\). This field is obtained by superposing two slightly displaced oppositely charged cylinders with \(q\mathbf s=-\mathbf P\), then taking their displacement to zero. Gauss's law gives \(\mathbf E_\mathrm{in}=-\mathbf P/(2\epsilon_0)\), and outside, for planar radius vector \(\mathbf r\),
\[\mathbf E_\mathrm{out}=\frac{R^2}{2\epsilon_0}\frac{2\mathbf r(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf P)-r^2\mathbf P}{r^4}.\]

Match the normal current across \(r=R\). The polarization surface charge \(\sigma=\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}\) must cancel the discontinuity in the normal motional current. This gives \(\mathbf P=\epsilon_0\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\). Therefore
\[\mathbf j_\mathrm{in}=\frac{\mathbf v\times\mathbf B}{2\varrho},\qquad \mathbf j_\mathrm{out}=\frac{R^2}{2\varrho r^4}\left[r^2\mathbf v-2\mathbf r(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v)\right]\times\mathbf B.\]
On the requested line \(x=0\), only \(j_x\) is nonzero:
\[j_x(y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{vB}{2\varrho},&|y|<R,\\-\dfrac{vBR^2}{2\varrho y^2},&|y|>R.\end{cases}\qquad j_y=j_z=0.\]

The ideal sharp field boundary permits the tangential-current jumps at the two rims. The inside and outside answer fields specify their open domains.
c. Required pulling force
Only current inside the magnetic patch experiences magnetic force. It is uniform, so integrate \(d\mathbf F=\mathbf j\times\mathbf B\,dV\) over volume \(\pi R^2\delta\):
\[\mathbf F_\mathrm{mag}=-\frac{\pi R^2\delta B^2}{2\varrho}\mathbf v,\qquad \mathbf F_\mathrm{pull}=\frac{\pi R^2\delta B^2v}{2\varrho}\hat{\mathbf y}.\]
Alternatively integrate Joule heating. Inside, \(P_\mathrm{in}=\varrho j_\mathrm{in}^2\pi R^2\delta=\pi R^2\delta v^2B^2/(4\varrho)\). Outside, \(j_\mathrm{out}^2=R^4v^2B^2/(4\varrho^2r^4)\), and integrating over annuli gives the same power. Thus \(F_\mathrm{pull}v=P_\mathrm{in}+P_\mathrm{out}\), confirming the force.
Source notes and validity
The source's current-conservation condition is written with a cross-product loop integral. The intended condition is \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf j=0\), equivalently zero net normal flux through a closed boundary. A separate circulation condition applies to the electric field. Several intermediate signs and dimensional factors in the source are typographical. The final currents and force above satisfy both boundary conditions.
The source also discusses a stepping-magnet Faraday model that happens to reproduce the in-plane current formulas but gives an incorrect electric field away from the plate. It is not a valid derivation of that three-dimensional field. In a correctly transformed continuously moving magnet, surface-charge fields cancel the external induced field. The streamlines outside the patch are circles tangent to the boundary: their tangency follows from \(2\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf r=r^2\), with \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf P=0\).

The assumed current is uniform through the plate thickness. Magnetic diffusion has diffusivity \(\varrho/\mu_0\), and the passage time is of order \(R/v\). Skin depth much greater than \(\delta\) requires \(\varrho R\gg\mu_0v\delta^2\). Original marking tables, the full discussion of the invalid alternative, and its partial-credit limits remain in the PDF.

children.text: A solid uniform cylinder of height \(h=10\,\mathrm{cm}\) and base area \(s=100\,\mathrm{cm^2}\) floats in a cylindrical beaker of height \(H=20\,\mathrm{cm}\) and inner bottom area \(S=102\,\mathrm{cm^2}\), filled with liquid. The cylinder-to-liquid density ratio is \(\gamma=0.70\). The cylinder bottom is a few centimetres above the beaker bottom. The cylinder oscillates vertically, its axis always coinciding with the beaker axis. The liquid-level oscillation amplitude is \(A=1\,\mathrm{mm}\).
Find the period \(T\). Neglect the liquid viscosity.

statement.text:
T1: Floating cylinder
A solid uniform cylinder of height \(h=10\,\mathrm{cm}\) and base area \(s=100\,\mathrm{cm^2}\) floats in a cylindrical beaker of height \(H=20\,\mathrm{cm}\) and inner bottom area \(S=102\,\mathrm{cm^2}\), filled with liquid. The cylinder-to-liquid density ratio is \(\gamma=0.70\). The cylinder bottom is a few centimetres above the beaker bottom. The cylinder oscillates vertically, its axis always coinciding with the beaker axis. The liquid-level oscillation amplitude is \(A=1\,\mathrm{mm}\).
Find the period \(T\). Neglect the liquid viscosity.

children.text: Let liquid density be \(\rho\). The equilibrium immersion depth is \(\gamma h\). If the cylinder moves down by \(x_1\) at speed \(v_1\), liquid in the narrow annular gap moves up by \(x_2\) at speed \(v_2\). Incompressibility gives

nodes.alt: Original equilibrium and displaced cylinder cross-sections, labelling areas s and S, densities gamma rho and rho, immersion gamma h, displacements x1 and x2, and opposite cylinder and annular-liquid speeds v1 and v2.

children.text: Moving liquid volume \(sx_1\) from below the cylinder into the upper gap raises its centre by \(\gamma h+(x_1+x_2)/2\). Combine this with the cylinder's gravitational-energy loss:
\[U=-\gamma\rho shg x_1+\rho s x_1g\left(\gamma h+\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\right)=\frac12\rho g\frac{sS}{S-s}x_1^2.\]

The gap speed is \(s/(S-s)=50\) times the cylinder speed. Liquid below the cylinder has speed of the cylinder's order, so its kinetic energy is negligible compared with the fast annular flow. The small amplitude also allows the annular column height to be replaced by \(\gamma h\). Including both the cylinder and gap liquid gives
\[k_{\rm eff}=\rho g\frac{sS}{S-s},\qquad m_{\rm eff}=\rho\gamma h\frac{sS}{S-s},\qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\gamma h}{g}}\simeq0.53\,\mathrm s.\]
Ignoring the liquid inertia would produce a much shorter, incorrect period. The result uses the narrow-gap and small-amplitude approximations justified by the supplied dimensions.

nodes.alt: Original dynamical cross-sections with upward cylinder acceleration a1, downward annular-liquid acceleration a2, atmospheric pressure p0 at the free surface and pressure p below the cylinder.

children.text: Let the displaced cylinder accelerate upwards at \(a_1\), while the gap liquid accelerates downwards at \(a_2\). Continuity gives \(s a_1=(S-s)a_2\). Applying Newton's law to a unit-area liquid column of height \(l=\gamma h+x_1+x_2\), and to the cylinder, gives
\[p_0-p+\rho gl=\rho l a_2,\qquad (p-p_0)s-\gamma\rho shg=\gamma\rho sh a_1.\]

Eliminate \(p\) and neglect products of small displacements and accelerations. Then \(\rho gs(x_1+x_2)=\gamma\rho sh(a_1+a_2)\). Continuity reduces this to \(a_1=gx_1/(\gamma h)\), opposite to the displacement. It is the same harmonic motion. Pressure is approximately uniform under the cylinder because horizontal liquid accelerations there are much smaller than those in the gap. Both original marking schemes remain in the reference PDF.

solution.text:
T1: Floating cylinder
Solution I: energy
Let liquid density be \(\rho\). The equilibrium immersion depth is \(\gamma h\). If the cylinder moves down by \(x_1\) at speed \(v_1\), liquid in the narrow annular gap moves up by \(x_2\) at speed \(v_2\). Incompressibility gives
\[s x_1=(S-s)x_2,\qquad s v_1=(S-s)v_2.\]

Moving liquid volume \(sx_1\) from below the cylinder into the upper gap raises its centre by \(\gamma h+(x_1+x_2)/2\). Combine this with the cylinder's gravitational-energy loss:
\[U=-\gamma\rho shg x_1+\rho s x_1g\left(\gamma h+\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\right)=\frac12\rho g\frac{sS}{S-s}x_1^2.\]
The gap speed is \(s/(S-s)=50\) times the cylinder speed. Liquid below the cylinder has speed of the cylinder's order, so its kinetic energy is negligible compared with the fast annular flow. The small amplitude also allows the annular column height to be replaced by \(\gamma h\). Including both the cylinder and gap liquid gives
\[K=\frac12\gamma\rho shv_1^2+\frac12\rho(S-s)\gamma h v_2^2=\frac12\rho\gamma h\frac{sS}{S-s}v_1^2.\]
\[k_{\rm eff}=\rho g\frac{sS}{S-s},\qquad m_{\rm eff}=\rho\gamma h\frac{sS}{S-s},\qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\gamma h}{g}}\simeq0.53\,\mathrm s.\]
Ignoring the liquid inertia would produce a much shorter, incorrect period. The result uses the narrow-gap and small-amplitude approximations justified by the supplied dimensions.
Solution II: dynamics

Let the displaced cylinder accelerate upwards at \(a_1\), while the gap liquid accelerates downwards at \(a_2\). Continuity gives \(s a_1=(S-s)a_2\). Applying Newton's law to a unit-area liquid column of height \(l=\gamma h+x_1+x_2\), and to the cylinder, gives
\[p_0-p+\rho gl=\rho l a_2,\qquad (p-p_0)s-\gamma\rho shg=\gamma\rho sh a_1.\]
Eliminate \(p\) and neglect products of small displacements and accelerations. Then \(\rho gs(x_1+x_2)=\gamma\rho sh(a_1+a_2)\). Continuity reduces this to \(a_1=gx_1/(\gamma h)\), opposite to the displacement. It is the same harmonic motion. Pressure is approximately uniform under the cylinder because horizontal liquid accelerations there are much smaller than those in the gap. Both original marking schemes remain in the reference PDF.

children.text: A resistor undergoes a phase transition. Its resistance is \(R_1\) below temperature \(T_c\), and \(R_2>R_1\) above \(T_c\). It is connected to a voltage source through an inductor of inductance \(L\). If the applied voltage lies between two critical values, \(V_1<V<V_2\), the resistor temperature oscillates.

nodes.alt: Original series circuit: voltage source V, inductor L and temperature-dependent resistor R.

children.text: Assume (i) the heat flux to the ambient medium is \(P=\alpha(T-T_0)\), where \(\alpha\) is constant and \(T_0\) is ambient temperature, and (ii) the resistor is small enough to reach thermal equilibrium much faster than \(L/R_2\).
Express \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) in terms of the supplied parameters.
Find the oscillation period when \(V=\sqrt{V_1V_2}\) and \(R_2=16R_1\).

statement.text:
T2: Thermal oscillations
A resistor undergoes a phase transition. Its resistance is \(R_1\) below temperature \(T_c\), and \(R_2>R_1\) above \(T_c\). It is connected to a voltage source through an inductor of inductance \(L\). If the applied voltage lies between two critical values, \(V_1<V<V_2\), the resistor temperature oscillates.

Assume (i) the heat flux to the ambient medium is \(P=\alpha(T-T_0)\), where \(\alpha\) is constant and \(T_0\) is ambient temperature, and (ii) the resistor is small enough to reach thermal equilibrium much faster than \(L/R_2\).
a
Express \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) in terms of the supplied parameters.
b
For \(V_1<V<V_2\), sketch qualitatively \(T(t)\), and find \((T_{\max}-T_0)/(T_{\min}-T_0)\).
c
Find the oscillation period when \(V=\sqrt{V_1V_2}\) and \(R_2=16R_1\).

children.text: At constant resistance \(R_j\), equilibrium requires \(V^2/R_j=\alpha(T_{\rm eq}-T_0)\). A nonoscillating state must have \(T_{\rm eq}<T_c\) on branch 1 or \(T_{\rm eq}>T_c\) on branch 2. Thus

Instantaneous thermal balance gives \(T=T_0+R I^2/\alpha\). Define switching currents \(I_1=\sqrt{\alpha(T_c-T_0)/R_1}\) and \(I_2=\sqrt{\alpha(T_c-T_0)/R_2}\), and branch equilibrium currents \(J_j=V/R_j\). On the low-resistance branch the current rises towards \(J_1>I_1\) with time constant \(L/R_1\). At \(I_1\), temperature reaches \(T_c\) and resistance switches to \(R_2\). Current is continuous across the switch, so temperature jumps upwards. It then decreases as current tends towards \(J_2<I_2\), with time constant \(L/R_2\). At \(I_2\), temperature reaches \(T_c\) from above and jumps down as resistance switches back to \(R_1\).

Original temperature and resistance versus time: temperature rises to Tc, jumps up at the switch to R2, decays to Tc and jumps down at the switch to R1. Axes T, R and t and the transition Tc are labelled.

On branch \(j\), with initial current \(I_{\rm start}\), \(I(t)=J_j+(I_{\rm start}-J_j)e^{-R_jt/L}\). The two branch durations give
The sketch remains self-review. The automatic fields check the two voltage thresholds, temperature ratio and period. Original detailed marking tables remain in the PDF.

solution.text:
T2: Thermal oscillations
a. Critical voltages
At constant resistance \(R_j\), equilibrium requires \(V^2/R_j=\alpha(T_{\rm eq}-T_0)\). A nonoscillating state must have \(T_{\rm eq}<T_c\) on branch 1 or \(T_{\rm eq}>T_c\) on branch 2. Thus
\[V_1=\sqrt{R_1\alpha(T_c-T_0)},\qquad V_2=\sqrt{R_2\alpha(T_c-T_0)}.\]
b. Temperature and current
Instantaneous thermal balance gives \(T=T_0+R I^2/\alpha\). Define switching currents \(I_1=\sqrt{\alpha(T_c-T_0)/R_1}\) and \(I_2=\sqrt{\alpha(T_c-T_0)/R_2}\), and branch equilibrium currents \(J_j=V/R_j\). On the low-resistance branch the current rises towards \(J_1>I_1\) with time constant \(L/R_1\). At \(I_1\), temperature reaches \(T_c\) and resistance switches to \(R_2\). Current is continuous across the switch, so temperature jumps upwards. It then decreases as current tends towards \(J_2<I_2\), with time constant \(L/R_2\). At \(I_2\), temperature reaches \(T_c\) from above and jumps down as resistance switches back to \(R_1\).


The ideal jumps represent the negligible thermal-response-time limit. Between switches \(I\) is an exponential relaxation, while \(T-T_0=R I^2/\alpha\) is proportional to its square. The extrema occur immediately after switching:
\[T_{\max}-T_0=\frac{R_2 I_1^2}{\alpha},\quad T_{\min}-T_0=\frac{R_1 I_2^2}{\alpha},\quad \frac{T_{\max}-T_0}{T_{\min}-T_0}=\left(\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right)^2.\]
c. Period
On branch \(j\), with initial current \(I_{\rm start}\), \(I(t)=J_j+(I_{\rm start}-J_j)e^{-R_jt/L}\). The two branch durations give
\[\mathcal T=\frac L{R_1}\ln\frac{I_2-J_1}{I_1-J_1}+\frac L{R_2}\ln\frac{I_1-J_2}{I_2-J_2}.\]
With \(\eta=R_2/R_1=16\), \(V=\eta^{1/4}\sqrt{R_1\alpha(T_c-T_0)}\). Hence \(I_2=I_1/4\), \(J_1=2I_1\), \(J_2=I_1/8\), and
\[\mathcal T=\frac L{R_1}\left[\ln\left(\frac74\right)+\frac1{16}\ln7\right]\simeq0.6812\frac L{R_1}.\]
The sketch remains self-review. The automatic fields check the two voltage thresholds, temperature ratio and period. Original detailed marking tables remain in the PDF.

solution.text:
T3: Dipole in a magnetic field
a. Uniform translation
Let \(\mathbf r\) point from the centre to the positive charge, and \(\mathbf p=2q\mathbf r\). The charge velocities are \(\mathbf v_\pm=\mathbf v\pm\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r\), so
\[\mathbf F=q(\mathbf v_+-\mathbf v_-)\times\mathbf B=2q(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r)\times\mathbf B=B\omega\mathbf p.\]

Constant centre velocity requires \(\omega=0\). The torque is \(\boldsymbol\tau=2q\mathbf r\times(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)=-2q\mathbf B(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v)\), so maintaining zero rotation also requires \(\mathbf v\perp\mathbf r\). Initially the dipole points along \(X\). Thus \(\omega_0=0\), and \(\mathbf v_0\) can point along either direction of \(Y\), with arbitrary speed. Zero velocity is also a stationary limiting case.
b. Circular orbit
For circular motion \(\mathbf F\) points towards the circle centre. Since \(\mathbf F\parallel\mathbf p\), the dipole remains radial and rotates with the orbital angular velocity \(\omega_0\). There is no torque because velocity is perpendicular to the rod. Centripetal balance gives \(2mv_0^2/R_c=pBv_0/R_c\). Therefore
\[\mathbf v_0=-\frac{qBd}{2m}\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad R_c=\frac{qBd}{2m|\omega_0|},\qquad (x_c,y_c)=\left(\frac{qBd}{2m\omega_0},0\right).\]

Here \(\omega_0\ne0\). Positive angular velocity places the centre on \(+X\), negative on \(-X\), while the initial velocity points downwards in both cases. The answer fields use \(w=|\omega_0|\) for radius, and signed \(\omega_0\) for \(x_c\).
c. Reversal threshold
Integrating \(2m\dot{\mathbf v}=\dot{\mathbf p}\times\mathbf B\) gives conserved generalized momentum \(2m\mathbf v-\mathbf p\times\mathbf B\). Starting from rest, reversal \(\mathbf p_1=-\mathbf p_0\) requires \(\mathbf v_1=-\mathbf p_0\times\mathbf B/m\), with speed \(qBd/m\). Magnetic forces do no work, so with \(I=md^2/2\),
\[\frac12 I\omega_0^2=\frac12 I\omega_1^2+m v_1^2.\]
The threshold occurs at \(\omega_1=0\). Thus \(\omega_{\min}=2qB/m\). Exactly at this threshold the reversed orientation is approached asymptotically. A complete reversal in finite time requires \(|\omega_0|>\omega_{\min}\). The word minimum in the source refers to this limiting threshold.
Alternative: pendulum equation
For dipole angle \(\theta\), the translational equations integrate to \(v_x=(qBd/2m)\sin\theta\), \(v_y=(qBd/2m)(1-\cos\theta)\). Substituting in the torque gives
\[\ddot\theta+\left(\frac{qB}{m}\right)^2\sin\theta=0.\]
This is the simple-pendulum equation. Reaching the inverted position needs the separatrix initial angular speed \(2qB/m\). Both signs of initial rotation have the same threshold magnitude.
d. Asymptote

At the limiting reversed orientation the angular speed tends to zero and the centre moves along \(+Y\). Generalized angular momentum about the origin is conserved:
\[L_{O,z}+B\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf p=\mathrm{const},\qquad L_{O,z}(0)=I\omega_{\min}=qBd^2.\]
On the asymptote \(x=D\), the translational angular momentum is \(2mD(qBd/m)=2qBdD\), while \(B\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf p=-BqdD\). Their sum is \(qBdD\), hence \(D=d\). Clockwise initial rotation gives asymptote \(x=-d\) and the same distance. Alternatively, on the separatrix \(\dot\theta=2(qB/m)\cos(\theta/2)\), so integrating \(dx/d\theta=(d/2)\sin(\theta/2)\) from 0 to \(\pi\) also gives \(D=d\). Original marking tables are in the PDF.

statement.text:

solution.text:
T1: A leak
a. Onset of leakage
Write \(p_u,T_u\) for upper-chamber variables and \(p_l,V_l,T_l\) for the lower ones. The upper volume remains \(V\). A fixed parcel of monatomic helium below the diaphragm is compressed adiabatically. With parcel volume \(v\),
\[0=p_l\,dv+d\left(\frac32p_lv\right)=\frac52p_l\,dv+\frac32v\,dp_l,\quad v^5p_l^3=\mathrm{const},\quad T_l^5p_l^{-2}=\mathrm{const}.\]
The diaphragm lifts enough to leak when the pressure difference balances its weight over area \(V/H\). Define
\[\Delta p=\frac{mgH}{V}=px,\qquad x=\frac{mgH}{pV},\qquad V_0=V(1+x)^{-3/5}.\]
b. Upper-chamber final temperature
During leakage \(p_l-p_u=\Delta p\) remains constant. Total gas energy conservation, including external piston work, is
\[0=p_l\,dV_l+\frac32d(p_uV+p_lV_l)=\frac52p_l\,d(V+V_l)+\frac32(V+V_l)\,dp_l.\]
\[(V+V_l)^5p_l^3=\mathrm{const}.\]
At leakage onset \(V_l=V_0\) and \(p_l=p(1+x)\). At piston contact \(V_l\to0\). Thus
\[p_l'=p\left[1+(1+x)^{3/5}\right]^{5/3},\qquad p_u'=p_l'-px.\]
All the gas, twice the initial mole number of either chamber, ends in the upper volume \(V\). Its equation of state gives
\[T_1=\frac T2\left(\left[1+(1+x)^{3/5}\right]^{5/3}-x\right).\]
c. Lower-chamber limiting temperature
Apply the parcel invariant \(T_l^5p_l^{-2}=T^5p^{-2}\) to the remaining lower gas as its amount tends to zero:
\[T_2=T\left(\frac{p_l'}p\right)^{2/5}=T\left[1+(1+x)^{3/5}\right]^{2/3}.\]
The original marking table is available in the reference PDF.

solution.text:
T2: Thread around a cylinder
Let \(P\) be the pulled point and \(O\) the top point of the loop. The loop is a non-planar curve with a cusp at \(P\). Cut the cylinder along the generator through \(P\) and unfold its side. Set the origin at \(O\), \(x\) around the circumference and \(z\) parallel to the axis in the pulling direction.


At impending axial slip, friction is parallel to \(z\), and the \(x\)-component of tension \(T_x\) is constant by force balance. A small segment has circumferential width \(dx\), angular span \(d\varphi=dx/R\), and normal reaction
\[dN=2T_x\sin(d\varphi/2)\simeq T_x\frac{dx}{R},\qquad df=\mu\,dN.\]
The \(z\)-components of the end tensions differ by \(T_xz''dx\). Balancing them against friction gives
\[T_xz''dx=df,\qquad z''=\frac\mu R,\qquad z(0)=z'(0)=0,\qquad z(x)=\frac{\mu x^2}{2R}.\]
The required loop length is the arc length across one full circumference on the unfolded surface:
\[L_0=2\int_0^{\pi R}\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\mu x}{R}\right)^2}\,dx=\frac{2R}{\mu}\int_0^{\pi\mu}\sqrt{1+\xi^2}\,d\xi.\]
\[L_0=\pi R\sqrt{1+(\pi\mu)^2}+\frac R\mu\operatorname{arcsinh}(\pi\mu).\]
A shorter loop cannot satisfy this force-balanced sliding geometry. As \(\mu\to0\), \(\operatorname{arcsinh}(\pi\mu)\sim\pi\mu\), so \(L_0\to2\pi R\), the circumference. The answer field uses the equivalent logarithmic form. Original marking tables remain in the PDF.

solution.text:
T3: Glass ball
a. Two images merging at a fold
For a point \(P\) on the thread and distant camera aperture \(A\), every ray reaching \(A\) lies in plane \(POA\), where \(O\) is the sphere centre. Let \(\alpha\) be the internal incidence angle at the exit surface and \(\beta\) the external angle. Geometry and Snell's law give
\[\gamma=2\alpha-\beta,\qquad n\sin\alpha=\sin\beta.\]

The function \(\gamma(\alpha)\) is not monotonic. Below its maximum \(\gamma_0\), two exit rays connect a given thread point to the observer. At the maximum the images merge. Thread points outside this accessible range are invisible. The two branches join at their endpoints and form the observed closed oval. A blue shadow marks missing red light and therefore probes the red index.
b. Red refractive index
At the fold, differentiating the two relations gives \(d\beta=2d\alpha\) and \(n\cos\alpha=2\cos\beta\). Combining with Snell's law gives
\[n^2=\sin^2\beta+4\cos^2\beta=4-3\sin^2\beta.\]

Find the point \(Q_0\) where a radius is tangent to the blue oval. If \(h=OQ_0\), its projected distance gives \(\sin\beta_0=h/R\). The photograph gives \(h/R\simeq0.765\). Thus
\[n_R=\sqrt{4-3(h/R)^2}\simeq1.498\simeq1.50.\]
c. Dispersion from the oval width
Directly subtracting two nearly equal index estimates has large relative error. Instead measure the blue oval's radial extent \(ST\simeq0.20R\). At the violet fold, red rays from the same thread point have internal angles \(\alpha_R=\alpha_V\pm\delta\), and external angles \(\beta_R=\beta_V\pm2\delta\), because \(\gamma\) is the same. Expand red Snell's law \((n_V-\Delta n)\sin(\alpha_V+\delta)=\sin(\beta_V+2\delta)\) through second order. The first-order terms cancel at the fold, leaving
\[\Delta n=\frac32n_V\delta^2,\qquad \frac{|ST|}{R}\simeq4\delta\cos\beta_V.\]
\[\Delta n\simeq\frac{3n_V}{32}\frac{|ST|^2}{R^2-h^2}\simeq0.0132\simeq0.013.\]
The source's violet-fold reading is approximately \(h/R=0.755\) and \(n_V=1.513\). Use the corresponding violet \(h\) in this width formula. The numerical fields allow the source's stated graph-reading uncertainties, but do not grade the diagram or derivation.
Alternative: solve the paired-ray equations

In the symmetry plane perpendicular to the thread define \(G_n(h)=\arcsin(h/R)-2\arcsin(h/(nR))\). Its non-monotonic dependence on \(h\) gives two images. Solving \(G_{n_R}(h_1)=G_{n_R}(h_4)\) gives \(n_R\simeq1.51\). Then solve \(G_{n_R}(h_{1,4})=G_{n_V}(h_{2,3})\) for all four pairings and average the violet indices. This yields \(n_V-n_R\simeq0.0145\), consistent with the first construction. Both methods and their original partial-credit tables are retained in the PDF.

solution.text:
T1: Solenoid and loop
a. Solution I: force on the loop
The stationary loop carries current \(J=\mathcal E/R\). Newton's third law gives the force on the solenoid as the opposite of the force on the loop. A long, thin solenoid can be represented externally by a north pole at \(O_1\) and a south pole at \(O_2\). Each pole has flux magnitude equal to the flux through a cross-section of the solenoid.
\[\Phi=B_{\rm in}A=\mu_0\frac{NI}{\ell}A.\]
With \(O_1=O\), the far pole is negligible. The near pole produces an outward radial field of magnitude
\[B(r)=\frac{\Phi}{4\pi r^2}=\frac{\mu_0NIA}{4\pi\ell r^2}.\]
Summing \(J\,d\mathbf l\times\mathbf B\) around the loop gives a force in the negative \(z\)-direction. The solenoid experiences the opposite force.
\[F_1=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}\,2\pi r\,B(r)=\frac{\mu_0NIA\mathcal E}{2\ell Rr},\qquad \mathbf F_1=F_1\mathbf e_z,\qquad \mathbf F_2=-F_1\mathbf e_z.\]
When \(O_2=O\), the radial field reverses, hence so does the force. The source also permits a hemisphere construction using half the internal field flux and half the spherical area. It gives the same radial field.
a. Solution II: force on a magnetic pole
The total magnetic moment is \(m=NIA\). Writing this as \(Q_m\ell\) gives the pole strength. The field at the centre of the battery-powered loop follows from the Biot-Savart law.
\[Q_m=\frac{NIA}{\ell}=\frac{\Phi}{\mu_0},\qquad B_{\rm loop}(0)=\frac{\mu_0J}{2r}=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E}{2Rr},\qquad F_1=Q_mB_{\rm loop}(0).\]
The north pole is pushed in the positive \(z\)-direction and the south pole in the negative direction. The pole analogy can also be justified by virtual work on the field energy: electric and magnetic energy densities are \(\varepsilon_0E^2/2\) and \(B^2/(2\mu_0)\), respectively. The substitutions \(\varepsilon_0^{-1}\leftrightarrow\mu_0\), \(E\leftrightarrow B\) and \(Q\leftrightarrow Q_m\) give
\[F_E=\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad F_B=\frac{\mu_0Q_m^2}{4\pi r^2},\qquad Q=\varepsilon_0\Psi\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad Q_m=\frac{\Phi}{\mu_0}.\]
a. Solution III: flux through the side
The loop field enters the near end of the solenoid with flux \(\Phi_{\rm in}=\mu_0\mathcal E A/(2Rr)\). Almost no flux escapes through the distant end, so it leaves through the side. For a circular turn with perimeter \(c=2\sqrt{\pi A}\), let \(B_i\) be the radial component at that turn. Its axial force is \(F_i=cIB_i\). Axial field components produce radial forces that cancel by symmetry.
\[F_1=I\frac N\ell\sum_i c\frac\ell N B_i=I\frac N\ell\Phi_{\rm in}=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E ANI}{2Rr\ell}.\]
a. Solution IV: integrate magnetic dipoles
A short segment has dipole moment \(d\mathbf m=IAN\,dz\,\mathbf e_z/\ell\). Its axial force is \(dm\,dB_{\rm loop}/dz\). Thus
\[B_{\rm loop}(z)=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E}{2R}\frac{r^2}{(z^2+r^2)^{3/2}},\qquad F_1=\frac{IAN}{\ell}\left[B_{\rm loop}(0)-B_{\rm loop}(-\ell)\right].\]
\[F_1=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E ANI r^2}{2R\ell}\left[\frac1{r^3}-\frac1{(\ell^2+r^2)^{3/2}}\right]\simeq\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E ANI}{2\ell Rr}.\]
A related construction uses Gauss's law for the magnetic field to obtain the radial flux through each segment from the change in axial field, then integrates the Lorentz force. It gives the same result.
a. Solution V: energy and the sources
Move the solenoid a small distance \(\delta z\) in the positive direction while an external force balances the magnetic force. The system includes its power supplies. The field energy alone is not the total energy.
\[-F_1\delta z=\delta E_{\rm total}=\delta E_{\rm field}+\delta E_{\rm sources}.\]
For this virtual displacement, replace the battery by a source holding \(J=\mathcal E/R\) constant. Only the mutual-inductance term changes.
\[E_{\rm field}=\frac12L_1I^2+\frac12L_2J^2+L_{12}IJ,\qquad \delta E_{\rm field}=IJ\,\delta L_{12}.\]
\[V_{\rm ind}^{\rm loop}=-I\frac{\delta L_{12}}{\delta t},\qquad V_{\rm ind}^{\rm solenoid}=-J\frac{\delta L_{12}}{\delta t},\qquad \delta E_{\rm sources}=-2IJ\,\delta L_{12}.\]
Consequently \(\delta E_{\rm total}=-\delta E_{\rm field}\) and \(F_1\delta z=IJ\,\delta L_{12}\). Moving a segment from the tail to the head changes the linked flux by
\[J\,\delta L_{21}=B_{\rm loop}(0)A\frac N\ell\delta z,\qquad L_{21}=L_{12},\qquad F_1=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E NAI}{2\ell Rr}.\]
With the tail at the centre, mutual inductance decreases and the force reverses. Without sources, superconducting circuits would conserve flux and their currents would change. Treating their field energy as if both currents were fixed gives the wrong sign.
The field-energy change can alternatively be evaluated by transferring a segment \(\delta z\) from tail to head, with \(\ell\gg\delta z\gg\sqrt A\). The internal solenoid field is \(B_{\rm sol}=\mu_0NI/\ell\), giving
\[\delta E_{\rm field}=\frac{A\delta z}{2\mu_0}\left[(B_{\rm loop}(0)+B_{\rm sol})^2-B_{\rm loop}(0)^2-B_{\rm sol}^2\right].\]
A third version uses the potential energy \(-\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf B\) of the transferred turns. This effective potential already includes the source-energy sign. The solenoid's own field is the same at both ends and cancels, while the distant loop field is negligible.
\[\delta E_{\rm pot}=-\frac{IAN\delta z}{\ell}\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E}{2Rr},\qquad F_1=-\frac{\delta E_{\rm pot}}{\delta z}.\]
b. Current and graph
Take \(t=0\) when the solenoid's centre passes \(O\). Then \(z_1=vt+\ell/2\) and \(z_2=vt-\ell/2\). Negligible self-inductance gives
\[J(t)=\frac{\mathcal E+V_{\rm ind}(t)}{R}.\]
Solution I uses the solid angles subtended by the loop at the two poles. The flux and its time derivative are
\[\Phi_{\rm loop}=\frac{\mu_0NIA}{2\ell}\left[\frac{z_1}{\sqrt{z_1^2+r^2}}-\frac{z_2}{\sqrt{z_2^2+r^2}}\right],\]
\[V_{\rm ind}=-\frac{d\Phi_{\rm loop}}{dt}=-\frac{v\mu_0NIA}{2\ell}\left[\frac{r^2}{(z_1^2+r^2)^{3/2}}-\frac{r^2}{(z_2^2+r^2)^{3/2}}\right].\]
Solution II uses reciprocity, \(L_{12}=L_{21}\). Temporarily hold a test loop current \(J_0\) fixed. Transferring a segment from tail to head gives
\[J_0\,dL_{21}=v\,dt\,\frac{NA}{\ell}\left[B_{\rm loop}(z_1)-B_{\rm loop}(z_2)\right],\qquad V_{\rm ind}=-I\frac{dL_{12}}{dt}.\]
Substituting the loop field gives the same expression. Transcription note: the source's intermediate prose drops the minus sign in \(V_{\rm ind}=I\dot L_{12}\) and labels a flux derivative with the reciprocal indices. The final negative derivative and the plotted current fix the intended sign and convention.
The deviation \(J-\mathcal E/R\) is odd in time. Initially the increasing flux reduces the current. Later the decreasing flux increases it. Far away, the solenoid field behaves as a dipole field, so \(V_{\rm ind}\) decays as \(|t|^{-4}\). Near the centre the deviation is small and approximately linear in \(t\). The dip and peak occur close to \(-\ell/(2v)\) and \(+\ell/(2v)\), with widths of order \(r/v\) and a separation approximately \(\ell/v\).
\[J_{\min}\simeq\frac{\mathcal E}{R}-\frac{v\mu_0NIA}{2Rr\ell},\qquad J_{\max}\simeq\frac{\mathcal E}{R}+\frac{v\mu_0NIA}{2Rr\ell}.\]
These extrema use \(\ell\gg r\), neglecting the other pole. The curve is smooth and locally quadratic about each extremum. The source's summary table abbreviates this quadratic behaviour without writing the nonzero extremal offset. The full formula above supplies that offset.

A massless thread makes \(N\) turns around a statically fixed cylinder, as shown in the figure. Initially, the free (unwound) ends of the thread are parallel to the axis \(X\). Then, a heavy point-like object \(P\) is attached to one end of the thread while the other end is pulled with a constant velocity \(u\) along \(X\). Find the maximum velocity attained by the heavy object.

The thread is inextensible and flexible. Suppose that the turns of the thread are wound tightly to one another and are placed practically in the same plane, perpendicular to the cylinder axis. Neglect any friction in the system. Do not consider the force of gravity.

solution.text:
T2: Mechanical accelerator

Solution I: rotating basis along the thread
Resolve the velocity into a longitudinal component along the thread and a transverse component. Let \(\mathbf e_1\) point from the cylinder toward \(P\), \(\mathbf e_2\) be perpendicular to it, and \(\varphi\) be the total turning angle measured from the initial thread direction. Inextensibility fixes \(v_l=-u\).
\[\mathbf v=-u\mathbf e_1+v_\perp\mathbf e_2,\qquad \dot{\mathbf e}_1=\dot\varphi\mathbf e_2,\qquad \dot{\mathbf e}_2=-\dot\varphi\mathbf e_1.\]
\[\mathbf a=-v_\perp\dot\varphi\mathbf e_1+(\dot v_\perp-u\dot\varphi)\mathbf e_2.\]
Tension is the only force and acts along the thread, so the perpendicular acceleration vanishes. Starting with zero transverse velocity gives
\[\dot v_\perp=u\dot\varphi,\qquad v_\perp=u\varphi.\]
At complete detachment, the thread has turned through \(2\pi N\). Hence
\[v_\perp=2\pi Nu,\qquad v_{\rm detach}=u\sqrt{1+(2\pi N)^2}.\]
Detachment does not give the maximum laboratory speed. After detachment, use the inertial frame translating with the pulled end at speed \(u\). The mass rotates around that end at constant relative speed \(2\pi Nu\), because tension does no work in that frame. The laboratory speed is maximal when the relative velocity points in the pulling direction, with the thread perpendicular to \(X\).
\[v_{\max}=u+2\pi Nu=u(2\pi N+1).\]
Solution II: a rotating reference frame
Let \(R\) be the cylinder radius and choose a frame rotating at \(\omega=u/R\). The wound thread is at rest in this frame. A point \(Q\) on the pulled end rotates relative to the cylinder with angular velocity \(-\omega\). The mass moves perpendicular to its unwound thread, so tension does no work in this frame. Coriolis force also does no work. Its kinetic-energy gain equals its loss of centrifugal potential energy.
\[\frac12mv_P^2=-\frac12m\omega^2R^2+\frac12m\omega^2r^2=\frac12m\omega^2l_P^2,\qquad v_P=\frac uR l_P,\qquad \omega_P=\frac{v_P}{l_P}=\omega.\]
Here \(r\) is the distance from the cylinder axis to \(P\) and \(l_P\) is its unwound thread length. The ends unwind symmetrically in the rotating frame, so their straight lengths are equal. At detachment,
\[l_P=\pi NR,\qquad v_P=\pi Nu.\]
Adding the rotating-frame velocity to \(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r\) gives the laboratory transverse component \(v_\perp=2v_P=2\pi Nu\). Continue in the translating frame after detachment as in Solution I to obtain \(v_{\max}=u(2\pi N+1)\).
Solution III: work and energy
Again \(v_l=-u\). The longitudinal acceleration is \(-v_\perp\dot\varphi\). If \(F\) denotes the signed longitudinal component of the tension, Newton's law and the work-energy theorem give
\[F=-mv_\perp\dot\varphi,\qquad \frac{dE_k}{dt}=Fv_l=mv_\perp\dot\varphi u,\qquad E_k=\frac12m(u^2+v_\perp^2).\]
Differentiating the last expression gives \(\dot v_\perp=u\dot\varphi\). The remainder is identical to Solution I. The signed \(F\) is negative because the actual tension points toward the cylinder, opposite to \(\mathbf e_1\).
The retained solution PDF contains the original partial-credit tables. The automatic field checks the maximum speed, including the motion after detachment.

statement.text:
T3: Cat eyes
You may have noticed that in darkness, when a cat is within the light beam of a headlamp, its eyes appear very bright, see the photo below (left). This phenomenon can be modelled by a lens setup, see the photo on right, and the diagram beneath the photos.


The photo on right was taken by a digital single-lens reflex camera. The light intensity at the camera sensor pixels marked by a red line (in the photo) is shown in the graph below: the log base 10 of the light intensity (measured as the number of photons caught by each pixel) is plotted against the \(x\)-coordinate, with the pixels' side length serving as the unit length.

The lens modelling cat eyes can be treated as an ideal thin lens of focal length \(f=55\,\mathrm{mm}\) and diameter \(D=39\,\mathrm{mm}\). However, you should keep in mind that the given graph shows real measurement data, and the lens has certain non-ideal features. Most importantly, partial reflections of brightly lit areas from the lens surfaces may decrease the contrast: dark areas seen through the lens appear less dark than they actually are. This effect can be neglected for the camera lens, but not so for the lens serving as a model of a cat's eye.
Based on the given data, estimate (with the accuracy of about 20 percent) the distance \(h\) between the axis of the camera and the axis of the lamp (which can be considered as a point source) if the distance of the camera from the paper sheet was \(L=4.8\,\mathrm m\).

children.text: The brightest region is the magnified image of the lamp's blur spot on the paper, seen through the lens. The paper lies slightly beyond the focal plane. The plateau at \(\log_{10}I=4.4\) indicates nearly uniform illumination of the spot. Its edge is sharp on the paper but blurred in the photograph, because the camera is focused on the lens, while the spot's image is between the lens and camera.

The second-brightest region, at \(\log_{10}I\simeq3.4\), is paper beside the blur spot, viewed through the lens. Ideally it would be dark because the lens shades it. Reflections and scattering by the glass brighten it. This scattered contribution is much weaker than the brightest plateau. Subtracting \(10^{3.4}\) from \(10^{4.4}\) can refine the estimate. The darkest region, with \(\log_{10}I<1.75\), is the black interior of the lens. The region \(x>420\), with \(\log_{10}I\simeq1.95\), is unobscured white paper.

Since \(L\gg f\) and the lens-to-paper distance \(d_0\) is of order \(f\), the lamp's illuminance is nearly the same at the lens and paper. solution.text:
T3: Cat eyes
Interpret the four brightness regions
The brightest region is the magnified image of the lamp's blur spot on the paper, seen through the lens. The paper lies slightly beyond the focal plane. The plateau at \(\log_{10}I=4.4\) indicates nearly uniform illumination of the spot. Its edge is sharp on the paper but blurred in the photograph, because the camera is focused on the lens, while the spot's image is between the lens and camera.
The second-brightest region, at \(\log_{10}I\simeq3.4\), is paper beside the blur spot, viewed through the lens. Ideally it would be dark because the lens shades it. Reflections and scattering by the glass brighten it. This scattered contribution is much weaker than the brightest plateau. Subtracting \(10^{3.4}\) from \(10^{4.4}\) can refine the estimate. The darkest region, with \(\log_{10}I<1.75\), is the black interior of the lens. The region \(x>420\), with \(\log_{10}I\simeq1.95\), is unobscured white paper.
Luminance and the blur-spot size
Since \(L\gg f\) and the lens-to-paper distance \(d_0\) is of order \(f\), the lamp's illuminance is nearly the same at the lens and paper. Let \(k\) be the ratio of the blur-spot area to the lens aperture area. The lens concentrates the received light onto that spot, so its luminance is \(1/k\) times that of the directly illuminated paper. A paraxial ideal lens preserves luminance, and the camera's sensor illuminance is proportional to source luminance. Thus
\[\frac1k=\frac{I_{\rm bright}}{I_{\rm paper}}\simeq10^{4.4-1.95}\simeq282,\qquad \sqrt k\simeq0.0596.\]
Explanation 1 from the source: a source of fixed area at distance \(a\) sends flux proportional to \(a^{-2}\) into the camera. Its image area is also proportional to \(a^{-2}\). Sensor illuminance, the flux divided by that image area, is independent of \(a\).
Explanation 2: a narrow cone of solid angle \(\omega\) carries flux \(\Phi\) from an area \(S\) on the blur spot. The lens images it onto \(S'=S(d_S/d_0)^2\). Similar triangles give \(\omega/\omega'=(d_S/d_0)^2\). Therefore the image luminance is \(\Phi/(S'\omega')=\Phi/(S\omega)\), equal to the spot luminance.
Find the paper and image distances
Write \(d_S\) for the distance from the lens to the image of the blur spot. Newton's lens formula gives
\[(d_S-f)(d_0-f)=f^2,\qquad d_S=\frac{d_0f}{d_0-f}.\]
Assume initially \(d_0-f\ll f\) and verify this afterward. The lamp image is a distance \(s\) beyond the focal plane, where \(s=f^2/(L-f-d_0)\simeq f^2/L\). Similar triangles give the physical blur-spot diameter \(D_{\rm BS}\) and its image diameter \(D_I\).
\[D_{\rm BS}=\frac{D(d_0-f-s)}{f+s}\simeq D\left(\frac{d_0-f}{f}-\frac fL\right),\qquad D_I=\frac{D_{\rm BS}d_S}{d_0}=\frac{D_{\rm BS}f}{d_0-f}.\]
\[D_I\simeq D\left[1-\frac{f^2}{L(d_0-f)}\right]\simeq\frac{D(L-d_S)}L.\]
Consequently the apparent angular diameters of the lens and spot image are equal: \(D_I/(L-d_S)=D/L\). This is also evident from the source's ray construction. Rays \(SAG\) and \(SBF\) connect the lamp to the edges of the blur spot. The intersection of \(SBF\) with \(FO\) gives image point \(J\), and the other edge gives \(H\). Their angular separation equals that of the aperture. Moving the viewing point from lamp to nearby camera changes these angles negligibly.
The area ratio gives \(\sqrt k=|D_{\rm BS}/D|\). Using the paraxial expressions from the source,
\[\pm\sqrt k=\frac1f\left(d_0-\frac{Lf}{L-f}\right)=\frac{d_0}f-\frac{L}{L-f}.\]
The two branches place the sheet on opposite sides of the lamp image. They give approximately \(d_0/f=1.07\) and \(0.95\). The observed real magnified spot image selects the branch beyond the lamp image, giving \(d_0/f\simeq1.07\) and \(d_S\simeq15.03f\simeq83\,\mathrm{cm}\). This verifies \(d_0-f\ll f\). The \(f/L\) correction should be retained here because it is not negligible relative to \(\sqrt k\).

\[\frac\theta{\theta_L}=\frac{hd_S}{D(L-d_S)},\qquad h=\frac{d_{\rm cr}}{D'}\frac{D(L-d_S)}{d_S}.\]
Here \(d_{\rm cr}\) is the crescent width and \(D'\) the lens aperture diameter in pixels. The graph gives a lens edge near \(x=30\), the midpoint of the blurry edge near \(120\), and the right lens edge near \(240\). Thus \(d_{\rm cr}\simeq90\) pixels and \(D'\simeq210\) pixels, yielding
\[h\simeq80\,\mathrm{mm}.\]

Under these conditions snow falling through the atmosphere (partially) melts in the warmer layer and (partially) freezes again before reaching the ground in the form of "ice pellets".

solution.text:
1. Ice pellets
a. Frozen mass fraction
With the given assumptions of constant droplet size and constant atmospheric density the drag force leads to a constant velocity \(v\) for the fall of the droplet through the atmosphere.
We can assume that the droplet temperature \(T_d\) above \(h_A\) follows the atmosphere temperature profile (also see below) and remains constant and equal to \(T_0=0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\) during the melting below that height.
For small temperature differences \(\Delta T=T-T_d\) the heat exchange rate is proportional to this difference \(dQ/dt=\kappa\Delta T\). The factor \(\kappa\) depends on the droplet geometry and its velocity, as well as on the air density. Since these are constant, \(\kappa=\mathrm{const}\).
In the region between \(h_A\) and \(h_B\) the droplet is therefore heated at a rate
\[dQ=\kappa(T-T_0)\,dt=-\kappa(T-T_0)\frac{dh}{v}.\tag{1}\]
The total heat transfer between \(h_A\) and \(h_B\) is
\[Q=\frac{\kappa A}{v}=mL,\tag{2}\]
where \(A=5.0\,\mathrm{km}\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\) is the area between the temperature curve and the height-axis in the region between heights \(h_A\) and \(h_B\). The right hand side equates the heat with the latent heat necessary to completely melt the ice droplet of mass \(m\).
In the region below \(h_B\) the liquid droplet partially freezes again. During this process the temperature is again constant. The mass fraction \(\eta\) of liquid freezing before reaching the ground can again be derived from the area \(A'=4.0\,\mathrm{km}\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\) between the curve and the height-axis.
\[Q'=-\frac{\kappa A'}{v}=-\eta mL.\tag{3}\]
Dividing (3) by (2) gives the mass fraction
\[\eta=\frac{A'}{A}=\frac45=0.80.\tag{4}\]
b. Ground temperature without inversion
If the temperature profile follows the dashed line the droplet will completely melt and the heat transferred from the atmosphere will heat it up. Since the latent heat of melting is much bigger than the specific heat of water times some degrees of temperature variation the temperature of the liquid droplet will closely follow the temperature of the atmosphere eventually. Its temperature at ground level should therefore be close to \(8\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\).
For a better estimate let us introduce a new coordinate \(x\) whose origin is at the height where the droplet is completely molten (somewhat higher than \(h_B\)), and which is oriented downwards. For the change in temperature of the droplet we then have
\[mc_{\rm water}\frac{dT_d}{dt}=mc_{\rm water}v\frac{dT_d}{dx}=\kappa(T-T_d),\tag{5}\]
where the temperature of the atmosphere is given by \(T(x)=T(x=0)+2.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\,\mathrm{km}^{-1}x=:T(x=0)+bx\). For the difference \(\Delta T=T-T_d\) between the atmospheric temperature and the droplet temperature we have
\[\frac{d\Delta T}{dx}=b-\frac{dT_d}{dx}=b-\frac{\kappa}{mc_{\rm water}v}\Delta T.\tag{6}\]
This differential equation is solved by
\[\Delta T=bx_0+\mathrm{const}\cdot\exp(-x/x_0),\tag{7}\]
where \(x_0=mc_{\rm water}v/\kappa\). From equation (2) we find \(mv/\kappa=A/L\), such that \(x_0=(c_{\rm water}/L)A\approx0.063\,\mathrm{km}\).
Therefore the exponential factor in the above equation is negligible at ground level (the constant is close to \(4\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\)) and we arrive at a temperature difference between the droplet temperature and the atmospheric temperature at ground level of
\[\Delta T\approx0.13\,{}^\circ\mathrm C,\qquad T_d\approx7.9\,{}^\circ\mathrm C.\tag{8}\]
Another phenomenon, which effectively shifts atmosphere temperature as it is "felt" by the droplet, is due to viscous dissipation. It can be estimated by equating the droplet potential energy loss rate \(mgv\) to thermal power carried away by the circumfluent air \(\kappa\Delta T^*\). This gives \(\Delta T^*\sim mgv/\kappa=gA/L=0.17\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\). If both corrections were taken into account, then the droplet temperature before hitting the ground would again be \(T_d\approx8.0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C\).
Answer convention: the official solution gives approximately 7.9 degrees Celsius with thermal lag alone and 8.0 degrees Celsius with the additional dissipation estimate. The numeric check accepts both within the stated 0.15 degree tolerance. Explain the approximation in your workings.

children.text: A solid, homogeneous spherical ball of mass \(m\) and radius \(R\) is made of insulating material and has charge \(Q\) distributed uniformly throughout its volume. The ball is placed on a large horizontal surface, and set in rolling motion without slipping in such a way that its center starts to move with initial horizontal velocity \(v_0\). There is a uniform magnetic field (flux density) of magnitude \(B\) perpendicular to the surface. The coefficient of static friction is large enough to prevent the ball from slipping on the surface. The moment of inertia of the ball about an axis through its center is \(2mR^2/5\).
Describe the motion of the center of the ball and the shape of its trajectory.
Hint: Depending on your approach you may use the following identity, valid for any three vectors \(\vec a\), \(\vec b\), and \(\vec c\).
\[\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec b(\vec a\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b).\]

statement.text:
2. Motion of a charged ball

The ball is placed on a large horizontal surface, and set in rolling motion without slipping in such a way that its center starts to move with initial horizontal velocity \(v_0\). There is a uniform magnetic field (flux density) of magnitude \(B\) perpendicular to the surface. The coefficient of static friction is large enough to prevent the ball from slipping on the surface. The moment of inertia of the ball about an axis through its center is \(2mR^2/5\).
Describe the motion of the center of the ball and the shape of its trajectory.
Hint: Depending on your approach you may use the following identity, valid for any three vectors \(\vec a\), \(\vec b\), and \(\vec c\).
\[\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec b(\vec a\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b).\]

children.text: The forces acting on the ball are the static frictional force \(\vec F\), the gravitational force, the normal force, and the Lorentz force \(\vec F_L\) caused by the magnetic field. None of these forces perform mechanical work on the ball, so the total kinetic energy of the ball is conserved. Due to the condition of pure rolling, the speed of the center of the ball \(v\) is proportional to the angular speed \(\omega\) of the rolling motion, i.e. the total kinetic energy can be expressed in terms of \(v^2\). As a result, the speed of the center of the ball remains constant, but the direction of velocity may change.
The net Lorentz force acting on the ball can be expressed with the help of the velocity of the center of the ball \(\vec v\):
This can be proven by summing up the magnetic forces acting on the small pieces of the ball.

Let us denote the charge of the ith small piece by \(\Delta Q_i\), the position vector directed from the center of the ball to the small piece by \(\vec x_i\). The velocity of this small piece is given by \(\vec v_i=\vec v+\vec\omega\times\vec x_i\), so the net Lorentz force can be written as
\[\vec F_L=\sum_i\Delta Q_i\vec v_i\times\vec B=\sum_i\Delta Q_i\vec v\times\vec B+\sum_i\Delta Q_i(\vec\omega\times\vec x_i)\times\vec B.\]

The second sum gives zero, because terms containing \(\vec x_i\) and \(-\vec x_i\) cancel each other pairwise. From the first sum \(\vec v\times\vec B\) can be taken out, so at the end the net force is the same as the Lorentz force acting on a point charge moving with the velocity of center of mass.

The speed of the center of the ball does not change, i.e. the net force (which is horizontal) should be perpendicular to the velocity \(\vec v\) of the center. Since the Lorentz force is always perpendicular to \(\vec v\), so should be the static frictional force \(\vec F\), as well. The magnitude of \(\vec F\) cannot depend on the position, only on the speed of the ball, so \(|\vec F|\) must remain constant during the motion. As a result, the net force (i.e. the acceleration of the center of the ball) is constant in magnitude, so the ball's center will perform a uniform circular motion with speed \(|\vec v|=v_0\) (see the Figure).

The magnitude of \(\vec F\) cannot depend on the position, only on the speed of the ball, so \(|\vec F|\) must remain constant during the motion. As a result, the net force (i.e. the acceleration of the center of the ball) is constant in magnitude, so the ball's center will perform a uniform circular motion with speed \(|\vec v|=v_0\) (see the Figure).

Now we can write down the equation of motion of the ball. The acceleration of the center of mass is horizontal, which is caused by the static frictional force and the net Lorentz force, so with the help of equation (1) Newton's 2nd law in the radial direction can be written as
\[QvB-F=mr\Omega^2,\tag{2}\]
where \(r\) is the radius of the circular trajectory of the center of mass and \(\Omega\) is the angular speed of the circular motion. We can obtain a relationship between the two angular speeds from the condition of pure rolling:
\[v_0=R\omega=r\Omega.\tag{3}\]
The magnetic field also exerts a net torque on the charged ball. The torque is given by
\[\vec\tau_L=\frac{Q}{2m}\vec L\times\vec B,\]
where \(\vec L\) is the angular momentum of the ball with respect to the center.
Proof 2. Magnetic torque
As the ball rolls on the surface, moving charges form loop currents which represent a net magnetic moment. A small piece of charge \(\Delta Q_i\) corresponds to current \(I_i=|\vec\omega|\Delta Q_i/(2\pi)\), so the contribution of this piece to the net magnetic moment \(\vec\mu\) has magnitude \(I_i\pi x_{i,\perp}^2\), where \(x_{i,\perp}\) is the distance of the small piece from the rotation axis of the ball. The direction of the net magnetic moment is parallel with the vector \(\vec\omega\), and its magnitude can be written as the sum
\[\vec\mu=\frac12\vec\omega\sum_i\Delta Q_i x_{i,\perp}^2.\]
Here we don't need to evaluate the sum (integral), if we use the analogy with the moment of inertia:
\[\sum_i\Delta m_i x_{i,\perp}^2=\frac25mR^2\quad\longrightarrow\quad\sum_i\Delta Q_i x_{i,\perp}^2=\frac25QR^2.\]
So the net magnetic torque acting on the ball (in the form of couples) is given by
\[\vec\tau_L=\vec\mu\times\vec B=\frac15QR^2\vec\omega\times\vec B=\frac{Q}{2m}\vec L\times\vec B.\]
The angular acceleration of the ball is caused by the frictional torque and the magnetic torque. As it can be seen from the Figure, both torques have the same direction, which is perpendicular to the ball's angular velocity. As a result, the axis of rotation of the ball precesses in the horizontal plane. To satisfy the condition of pure rolling, the angular speed of the precession must be \(\Omega\). During precession the rate of change of the angular momentum is given by \(|\vec L|\Omega\), so the equation of rotational motion for the center of the ball is
\[\underbrace{\frac15QR^2\omega B}_{|\vec\tau_L|}+RF=\underbrace{\frac25mR^2\omega}_{|\vec L|}\Omega.\tag{4}\]
From equations (2), (3) and (4) the radius and the angular velocity of the circular motion can be expressed:
\[r=\frac76\frac{mv_0}{QB},\qquad\Omega=\frac67\frac{QB}{m}.\]
Answer convention: the scalar radius and angular-speed fields use positive Q for the magnitude of the charge. Reversing the sign of the charge reverses the circulation direction. The qualitative description is for self-review.

This fact can be proved as follows (the proof is not required from the contestants). The trajectory of the ball can be expressed parametrically as \(x=v\cos\alpha\,t\), \(y=v\sin\alpha\,t-\tfrac12gt^2\). Upon eliminating \(t\) we obtain
We can consider this as an equation for finding the angle \(\alpha\) to reach the point \((x,y)\):

The points at the envelope separate the points for which the solution to this equation does exist from the points for which the solution does not exist, hence for the envelope points the discriminant of the equation must be zero,

What we got is a parabola, and the position of the focus can be deduced from this formula. Alternatively, the position of the focus can be deduced from the fact that light rays parallel to the axis of a parabola converge after reflection from the parabolic shape into its focus. Indeed, the touching point of the envelope with a trajectory of a ball launched at \(\alpha=45^\circ\) must lie at \(y=0\) as this launching angle is known to provide the longest flight distance. Hence, the envelope and the x-axis meet at \(45^\circ\), so that a vertical beam hitting the envelope at \(y=0\) is reflected by the envelope into a horizontal line. The focus must lie on that reflected beam, i.e. at \(y=0\).

The parabolic trajectory of each water parcel must touch the envelope (1 pt). Using the knowledge that the launching angles of the water parcels were never less than \(45^\circ\), we conclude that the touching point must lie at \(y\ge0\) (1 pt). This can be seen from the fact that a parcel launched at \(45^\circ\) will meet the envelope at \(y=0\), and increasing the launching angle will raise the touching point.

There are many ways of proving it more rigorously. For instance, one can use the fact (proved below) that the launching velocity and the tangent to the envelope at the point \(A\) where the trajectory and the envelope meet are perpendicular to each other: with \(\alpha+\beta=90^\circ\) (\(\beta\) denotes the angle between the tangent to the horizon) we conclude that increasing \(\alpha\) means decreasing \(\beta\), which is to say that the touching point \(A\) gets higher.

To prove the equality \(\alpha+\beta=90^\circ\), let a vertical light beam be reflected from the trajectory at \(A\): it will go through the focus of the trajectory which means that if we continue it through the focus and let it be reflected a second time from the same trajectory, it will propagate vertically down. The trajectory and the envelope are tangent at \(A\), so the first reflection was also a reflection from the envelope and the reflected beam must go through the focus of the envelope, i.e. the launching point \(O\). Point \(O\) lies on the trajectory, so the second reflection point must be \(O\). As a result of the two reflections, the beam was diverted by \(180^\circ\) which means that the double sum of the incidence angles must have been \(180^\circ\), and hence \(2\alpha+2\beta=180^\circ\).
Locating the envelope on the plotted stream

The water parcels close to the origin are clearly yet to reach the envelope, and those parcels below the ground level have clearly passed the point where they touched the envelope. Since the parcels form a continuous curve, there must be at least one point \(P\) which is exactly at the envelope (1 pt).

There are two ways of finding the position of the point \(P\). The first approach is as follows. Notice that at \(P\), the water curve is tangent to the envelope (1 pt). Hence, a vertical line drawn through \(P\) will be reflected by the water curve so that it will go through the focus \(O\) (1 pt). So, we need to find by trial and error such a point \(P\) on the upper segment of the water curve that the line \(OP\) and a vertical line drawn through \(P\) will form equal angles with the water curve at \(P\) (finding the position of \(P\) with a reasonable accuracy: 1 pt), see the figure below.

Alternatively, we can use the fact that for any point on a parabola, its distance from the focus plus its distance from a horizontal line is constant. So, for an arbitrary point \(Q=(x,y)\) on the envelope, \(y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=2H\), where \(H\) is a constant, and for any point beneath it, \(y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<2H\). Hence, among all the points at the water curve, the point \(P\) has the largest value of \(y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) (2 pts). We can evaluate \(y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) for a series of points at the water curve and find the one with the largest value (finding the position of \(P\) with a reasonable accuracy: 1 pt).

The topmost point of the envelope would be reached by a water parcel launched vertically, so \(v^2=2gH_P\), and \(v=\sqrt{2gH_P}\) (1 pt). From the figure we can find \(2H_P=(3.3+\sqrt{10.8^2+3.3^2})\,\mathrm m\approx14.6\,\mathrm m\) so that \(v\approx12\,\mathrm{m/s}\) (1 pt).
